title: Xgimi’s New Aura 3 UST Projectors Get Bright and Look Classy
snippet: With 120Hz refresh and a reasonable price, the Aura 3 Max and Pro could be very interesting.
fullText:
At IFA in Berlin, Xgimi unveiled a pair of new ultrashort-throw projectors. Called the Aura 3 Max and Aura 3 Pro, they slot in above the Aura 2 in Xgimi’s range. Like several new projectors, notably from AWOL and JMGO, the Aura 3 models have high brightness and 120Hz refresh rates. 

The classy, wood-paneled design holds a light engine capable of a stated 5,700 lumens in the Max and 4,100 in the Pro. Xgimi also says the Aura 3s have the world’s first dual iris system, giving greater control over the amount of light hitting the screen. 

This dynamic contrast ratio isn’t quite as eye-catching as a high native contrast ratio, but I won’t be able to judge that until I get one in my lab for testing. Xgimi says it’s the same light engine as what’s in the Titan Noir, so I’d expect solid performance.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The designs are similar to the Aura 3. Xgimi had them set up on the floor, which would certainly work if you don’t have kids, clumsy adults or curious pets. UST projectors are typically designed to be the central hub of a home cinema, and as such the internal speakers play an important role. For the Aura 3 series, Xgimi has again partnered with Harman Kardon for assistance with the audio. Both models have 80 watts total, though the company hasn’t announced how many drivers those watts power.

Also shown with the Aura 3 at Xgimi’s IFA booth was the (maybe) production version of the Ascend screen I first saw at CES 2025. It’s a stylish, motorized ambient-light-rejecting screen. 

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

Xgimi announced preorder pricing via Kickstarter. I’m not a fan of preorders in general and definitely not big companies using Kickstarter. It said a $50 deposit will get you $200 off, with the preorder price being $2,399 for the Max and $2,199 for the Pro. That’s a little higher than the Aura 2, which itself performs quite well for the price. The actual MSRP will likely be higher at launch.

title: Apple Vision Pro was just used in a first-of-its-kind surgery
snippet: We’ve seen several stories about Apple Vision Pro being used in healthcare settings. This week, Stryker announced the completion of the first surgical procedure using an innovative new app on Vision Pro. more…
fullText:
We’ve seen several stories about Apple Vision Pro being used in healthcare settings. This week, Stryker announced the completion of the first surgical procedure using an innovative new app on Vision Pro.

The surgery, a hip arthroscopy, was completed using SportSuite Vision, an app that brings “critical digital content into a surgeon’s virtual space.” This includes things like arthroscopic video, HipCheck, HipMap, and CT imaging.

Here’s how Stryker describes the app:

SportSuite Vision brings critical digital content into a surgeon’s visual space, allowing them to see physical objects in the OR alongside digital tools such as arthroscopic images, HipCheck, HipMap and CT imaging.

During arthroscopic procedures, surgeons often rely on multiple displays positioned throughout the OR to access visualization and procedural data. By bringing multiple data sources into the surgeon’s field of view, the technology can reduce reliance on traditional monitors and support a more streamlined, ergonomic surgical workflow.

SportSuite Vision received FDA De Novo authorization on July 17. Stryker says this makes it the first app the FDA has authorized for intraoperative use with Vision Pro.

The hip arthroscopy was completed at Duke Health. Chad Mather III, the orthopedic surgeon who performed the operation, praised Vision Pro and SportSuite Vision:

“Using spatial computing enabled me to customize the placement of key clinical information to fit my workflow and access it within the sterile field. This helped create a more comfortable, streamlined OR setup while keeping the information I needed in view.”

You can learn more about SportSuite Vision on the Stryker website.

Also this week, Pfizer announced it is using Apple Vision Pro “to create an unforgettable, immersive experience” to “illustrate” its commitment to “outdo cancer.”

Pfizer’s bold mission is clear: Outdo cancer through relentless innovation and hope. To vividly illustrate this commitment for patients, healthcare providers, and internal stakeholders, Pfizer collaborated with Groove Jones to craft an immersive mixed reality experience that inspires as much as it informs. Apple Vision Pro’s ability to seamlessly blend digital and real worlds provided the perfect canvas to emotionally connect audiences and showcase Pfizer’s oncology leadership.

You can get a closer look at the experience on the Groove Jones website.

title: Three new iPhones launch this week, here’s what’s coming
snippet: Apple’s big September event is this Wednesday, and the company has three new iPhone models set to launch: iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Ultra. Here’s what to expect. more…
fullText:
Apple’s big September event is this Wednesday, and the company has three new iPhone models set to launch: iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone 18 Pro Max, and iPhone Ultra. Here’s what to expect.

iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max

iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are coming as successors to Apple’s popular 17 Pro line.

New features that are rumored include:

A20 Pro chip for more power and efficiency

Major camera upgrades, especially to the Main camera with variable aperture

35% smaller Dynamic Island for more modern design

New colors, headlined by a bold burgundy

Best battery life ever, with iPhone 18 Pro Max getting big gains

Camera Control gets a revamp

C2 cellular modem designed by Apple

New satellite features, including 5G

iPhone 18 Pro is also expected to have a higher starting price. Estimates suggest it could start at $1,399, but I suspect it could be closer to $1,199 or $1,249.

iPhone Ultra

iPhone Ultra is the rumored name for Apple’s first foldable, with its expected $2,000+ price creating a new high-end tier.

The foldable form factor should make iPhone Ultra the most radically unique model Apple has yet introduced. It will have a wide book-style fold, with a roughly 5.4-inch outer display and 7.8-inch inner display that resembles an iPad mini.

Design materials are expected to mimic the iPhone Air, with a titanium border and sleek look.

iPhone Ultra will have two rear cameras (Main and Ultra Wide) plus two front-facing cameras, one for each display. It will use Touch ID for authentication rather than Face ID.

Software will be where the device especially shines, with iOS 27 supporting side-by-side app multitasking and adaptive landscape layouts that are perfect for the new form factor.

Performance should be about the same as iPhone 18 Pro, with the same A20 Pro chip, a vapor chamber for cooling, and a C2 modem.

What’s missing: iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2

Normally we would expect a new base model iPhone 18 to launch in September too, alongside an iPhone Air successor.

This year though, Apple is reportedly overhauling its fall lineup by pushing the iPhone 18 and iPhone Air 2 into early 2027.

It’s unknown whether this change is entirely strategic, or simply out of necessity due to the current memory crisis. In any case, the absence of more affordable models means this fall’s new iPhone line will focus solely on the high end.

title: Gemini 3.8 Flash rolling out three weeks after last release
snippet: After the last model release three weeks ago, Google today is rolling out Gemini 3.8 Flash. This marks the third Flash update in three months. more…
fullText:
After the last model release three weeks ago, Google today is rolling out Gemini 3.8 Flash. This marks the third Flash update in three months.

…our most intelligent workhorse model, delivering significant improvements from 3.7 Flash across software engineering, agentic tasks, and critical, multi-step reasoning in specialized domains.

Gemini 3.8 Flash “delivers substantial gains” over its predecessor in various benchmarks, with Google also noting how it is “often approaching the performance of higher-cost frontier models.”

On DeepSWE v1.1 (Long-Horizon Software Engineering) 3.8 Flash outperforms most larger frontier models in autonomously solving complex engineering problems end to end, only at a fraction of the cost.

In quantitative and professional fields that require advanced analysis and reporting, 3.8 Flash outperforms 3.7 Flash and other frontier models in benchmarks like Vals Finance Agent V2 and Harvey’s Legal Agent Benchmark. 

3.8 Flash also achieves a 54.9% on HLE-Verified, demonstrating its ability to handle multi-step reasoning across STEM, humanities, and professional fields.

Google says these “performance gains stem from a core design choice: 3.8 Flash works harder.”

On complex tasks, it exhibits greater diligence — executing extra reasoning steps, and calling tools iteratively. At times, the model might use more tokens to maximize performance, especially at higher effort levels.

Note: Updated DeepSWE v1.1 score

	

Similar to the previous model, Gemini 3.8 Flash’s knowledge cutoff date is March 2026 “for some domains while in others [users] may experience the model’s knowledge is limited to January 2025.”

Google is once again offering an introductory price of $0.75/1M input tokens and $3.75/1M output tokens until December 31.

Gemini 3.8 Flash is already live in the Gemini app for Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers, AI Mode, and Gemini in Google Sheets. It’s also available for developers in Google Antigravity, AI Studio, and the Gemini API.

Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber

Google today also announced Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber (replacing 3.5) for trusted testers — via a new Fairwind Program — with “frontier-level performance in autonomous vulnerability discovery.”

The Chrome Security team found that 3.8 Flash Cyber produced 2.6 times more correct patches to vulnerabilities in Chrome than the best commercial models that are much larger.

Wiz found that Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber achieves +7.5-9.7% higher recall on their internal penetration testing benchmark for a 2.3-5.2x lower cost compared to other leading frontier models.

Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research team leveraged the 3.8 Flash Cyber model to find a critical foundational vulnerability in less than 2 hours, a vulnerability for which research and discovery usually takes months.

title: Google stops selling ‘Certified Refurbished’ Pixel 7 series, still no Pixel 9 yet
snippet: Google has pulled refurbished Pixel 7 devices from its store, with the Pixel 9 yet to make its debut. more…
fullText:
Google has pulled refurbished Pixel 7 devices from its store, with the Pixel 9 yet to make its debut.

On the Google Store you can buy a “Certified Refurbished” Pixel smartphone at a lower price, usually hundreds off of the original retail price. While it’s not always the best deal compared to a used device on the private market, there’s considerable peace of mind in buying a refurbished device directly from Google seeing as every device comes with a one-year warranty, gets a full inspection with replacement parts, and is sold unlocked for use with any carrier. These devices are also available on Amazon.

But the options have now shrunk.

Google now only has the Pixel 8 series – 8, Pro, and 8a – available alongside the Pixel 7a, with prices ranging from $289 to $649. The Pixel 7 series has been removed in the past few days, with its final appearance on the Wayback Machine in late August. Google was running a promotion where refurbished Pixel 7 devices included a free Pixel Watch 2 from July up until the past week or so.

	

This doesn’t come as a huge surprise. The Pixel 7 series launched in 2022 and will stop getting updates in the latter half of 2027. What’s more of a surprise is that the Pixel 9 series has yet to arrive in Google’s refurbished program. With Pixel 11 now available, it’s likely the Pixel 9 will arrive in the coming weeks. Pixel 8 was added in October 2025, roughly two months after the Pixel 10’s debut.

title: Google Pixel adding ‘Battery usage summaries,’ rolling out on Pixel 10 and newer
snippet: Google is rolling out a new AI-generated feature on Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 devices called “Battery usage summaries” which translate battery use stats into natural language. more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out a new AI-generated feature on Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 devices called “Battery usage summaries” which translate battery use stats into natural language.

Rolling out via an AI Core update on Pixel 10 and Pixel 11 devices, “Battery usage summaries” deliver on a rather simple premise. On your battery usage page, a new AI-generated overview summarizes your battery usage, pulling in recent history and calling out more powerful apps. 

On a support page, Google explains:

At the top of the Battery usage page, you can get a personalized summary of your battery usage. It summarizes these analyses, which are performed in the background:

Identifies apps that consume the most battery.

Monitors app background activity.

Compares the overall and app-specific battery consumption between your selected period and recent average.

The feature is enabled by default on supported Pixels, but can be turned off via Settings > Battery & charging > Battery Usage > Battery usage summaries (overflow menu). A screenshot sent to Android Authority shows an example of what the summary might say beyond the “you’ve barely used your phone” vibes our unused-for-the-day Pixel 11 Pro Fold shows. Google says that “outputs vary and highlight the most important info only.”

	

Google’s support page mentions that the latest AI Core update is needed to enable the feature, but it’s unclear if there are any additional requirements. While we’re seeing the feature live on both a Pixel 11 Pro Fold and a Pixel 11 Pro XL, it’s not yet showing on Pixel 10 or Pixel 10a devices we’ve updated and tested.

If you’re seeing “Battery usage summaries” on your Pixel, let us know in the comments below.

title: FBI investigates as hackers sell digital scans of 153M drivers licenses
snippet: The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is reportedly investigating identity theft as digital scans of more than 153 million driver’s licenses went on sale on the dark web. Additional documents offered through a massive security breach include medical cards, residence cards, and more. The licenses belong to people in the US and Canada, and appear to have been collected by hacking an identity verification service … more…
fullText:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is reportedly investigating identity theft as digital scans of more than 153 million driver’s licenses went on sale on the dark web. Additional documents offered through a massive security breach include medical cards, residence cards, and more.

The licenses belong to people in the US and Canada, and appear to have been collected by hacking an identity verification service … 

Krebs on Security was able to confirm the authenticity of the claim made by the cybercriminals as they were able to provide a scan of his own driving license, with other victims likewise confirming their scans were correct.

A new identity theft service [dubbed Nexus] launched on the dark web this week is selling digital scans of more than 153 million drivers licenses from people in the United States and Canada […] The people behind Nexus claim the license images are coming from an active breach at “a major identity verification company” whose customers include multiple Fortune 500 companies.

KrebsOnSecurity also has learned that the New Orleans field office of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) today launched an official inquiry into the source of the images.

The report says that the ID verification company appears to be one based in Louisiana. The criminals claim that they still have access to the source of these scans, a claim supported by their adding almost 400,000 new ones within the past 24 hours.

There are indications suggesting that at least some of the data was stolen from a verification service used by rental car company Hertz. The report points to a New Orleans-based company as a potential source, and that company’s client list includes Hertz, Target, Fedex, Motorola Solutions, Jack Henry, and Caesars Entertainment. There are many more details in the full report.

title: Oura is going public, but these smart ring companies are coming for its crown
snippet: While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, a growing number of rivals are now racing to dethrone it by trying all sorts of approaches to get an edge over it.
fullText:
The smart ring market is getting crowded, and Oura isn’t waiting around to see what happens next: It officially filed to go public on September 3.

The company is killing it right now. The Finnish outfit’s revenue nearly doubled to $1.21 billion for the nine months ended June 30. Oura said it sold 3.6 million rings over the past year and that it has around 5 million paid members. The company’s move to go public follows the recent launch of the Oura Ring 5, its slimmest and lightest ring yet.

But while Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals are emerging from all corners to dethrone it, each betting on a different angle. For example, French company Circular announced this week that its upcoming ring will allow users to tap to pay with their ring, while Chinese company RingConn debuted a ring this year that added haptic vibrations. 

Indian company Ultrahuman separately announced this week that it raised $70 million with backing from Qualcomm’s venture arm as it looks to build a ring that it says will be able to run software directly on the device and eventually power everything from AI interactions to games.

The race to beat Oura isn’t just about enhanced health and sleep tracking anymore. It’s now about seeing which company can cram the most smartphone-like features into a two-gram titanium band before someone ends up shipping a ring that lets you doomscroll TikTok or answer calls or do your taxes. I mean, we’re already seeing smart rings with screens, like the Pebble Halo, although it’s currently only available in India, as well as rings that promise touchpads, like the Dreame Ring.

The irony is that the initial appeal with smart rings was that they made technology and health tracking feel less intrusive than devices like smartwatches and smartphones, given you can step away from a screen while still keeping tabs on your health. With the way things are headed in the smart ring industry, though, we may just end up slipping mini smartphones on our fingers.

All of this is to say that the smart ring market is getting increasingly confusing, so we’ve rounded up the most notable contenders vying for Oura’s crown. 

Ultrahuman

Image Credits:Ultrahuman

Earlier this year, Ultrahuman unveiled its third-generation smart ring, the $479 Ring Pro, which is set to begin shipping in the U.S. in mid-September. Ultrahuman’s U.S. business was disrupted in October 2025 after the U.S. International Trade Commission ruled in Oura’s favor in a patent dispute. The ruling prevented the company from importing new ring inventory into the country, so Ultrahuman developed the Ring Pro with a redesigned form factor in order to circumvent Oura’s patent.

The Ring Pro features a redesigned heart-rate sensing system aimed at improving signal quality during sleep, along with a new dual-core processor that enables more accurate data collection and greater on-device processing. As noted earlier, Ultrahuman looks to be more ambitious with future rings as it aims to go beyond sleep and health tracking. 

Circular

Image Credits:Circular

Circular’s upcoming Ring 3 series, which consists of a Pro model and a Slim option, is expected to launch early next year. Both of the smart rings will feature an integrated NFC chip for contactless payments and on-finger vibrations that can be used for silent wake-up alarms, reminders, vital health alerts, and more. 

The Ring 3 Pro features a slimmer design than its predecessor and comes with FDA-cleared ECG for A-fib detection, blood pressure trend tracking, glucose tracking, advanced sleep analysis, and comprehensive biometric monitoring.

Pricing for the upcoming rings is not yet available. 

RingConn

Image Credits:RingConn

The RingConn Gen 3, which launched in May and starts at $349, features vascular health insights that use sensor data from the ring to assess changes in vascular strain over time after calibration with externally measured blood pressure values.

It also tracks heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, sleep, activity, and stress, among other metrics. Additionally, it features vibration alerts for health changes, sedentary reminders, and low battery. Unlike Circular, which leans on haptics to make its ring more communicative, RingConn mostly sticks to vibration as a health-alert mechanism.

Samsung

Image Credits:Samsung

Samsung became the first major tech giant to launch a smart ring in 2024. The Galaxy Ring, which costs $399, is arguably the strongest contender for anyone already invested in Samsung’s ecosystem of devices. 

Compared with other smart rings on the market, the Galaxy Ring is relatively basic when it comes to advanced health and sleep tracking. It lacks features such as sleep apnea detection, which are offered by RingConn, Oura, and Ultrahuman, as well as A-fib detection, which is available on Circular and RingConn smart rings. 

Dreame

Image Credits:Dreame

Dreame, a relatively new entrant to the smart ring market, unveiled a ring earlier this year with haptic alerts for alarms, calls, messages, and more, along with a small touchpad that lets you do things like skip a song or snap a photo on your phone. It’s also said to offer heart rate tracking, blood oxygen monitoring, heart rate variability insights, sleep analysis, and more.

Pricing and availability have yet to be announced.

iPhone 18 Pro is launching next week, and expected to feature three upgrades that have been rumored for years. Here’s what’s coming.

It’s been more than two years since The Information published a report detailing a “variable aperture” camera system coming to iPhone. At the time, it claimed iPhone 17 was the target model for the new feature. Ming Chi-Kuo, however, chimed in that it was instead set for the iPhone 18 line.

Now, iPhone 18 Pro is almost here and the latest reporting indicates variable aperture is indeed coming to the Main camera—at least on Pro Max, if not both models.

The new feature could unlock a variety of exciting camera abilities, but it all depends on Apple’s implementation. Fortunately we’re just days away from the unveiling and full feature reveal.

It’s been almost 10 years since the iPhone X introduced the notch, the first cutout in an iPhone display. It wasn’t until 2022’s iPhone 14 Pro that the current Dynamic Island design arrived, shrinking the cutout.

Now four years later, a smaller Dynamic Island is finally coming with iPhone 18 Pro.

Rumors indicate Apple’s new Dynamic Island cutout will be about 35% smaller than the previous design. This reduction in size is even hinted at by Siri’s new look in iOS 27.

title: Apple might soon make App Store changes to raise revenue, increase margins: report
snippet: According to the latest edition of the Power On newsletter from Mark Gurman, Apple is reportedly considering making some changes to its App Store. The goal? To increase the potential revenue it brings in. more…
fullText:
According to the latest edition of the Power On newsletter from Mark Gurman, Apple is reportedly considering making some changes to its App Store. The goal? To increase the potential revenue it brings in.

It isn’t exactly clear what changes Apple could have planned for the App Store. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports that Apple wants to “figure out ways to raise margins and squeeze additional recurring revenue from the platform,” and that this effort is largely driven by new CEO John Ternus and existing services SVP Eddy Cue.

Supposedly, this effort was part of the reason why longtime Apple executive Phil Schiller left the company last week. After departing from his role as marketing SVP in 2020, Schiller became an Apple Fellow – where part of his role was running the App Store. Schiller wasn’t a fan of the idea:

Schiller, on the other hand, seems to believe that such moves will only further irk developers and governments. While there was no internal blowup or anything like that, it’s something he wanted no part of.

There’s a multitude of ways Apple could potentially raise margins from the App Store. It could get rid of its manual app review process, which is likely costly and not super effective in the age of agentic coding. People likely wouldn’t appreciate further automation of app review, though it would certainly be a way to cut on costs.

	

It could charge more for its developer membership, currently priced at $99/year. Given the fact that many small developers are spending $200/mo for Codex and Claude subscriptions to develop apps, you could argue Apple could charge more and get away with it. The company could also charge large developers a subscription fee based on traffic, to offload some of the infrastructure costs.

Only time can tell what this will turn into, though I’m certainly interested to see what the changes could possibly look like.

title: Should You Buy a New iPhone From Apple, a Carrier or Unlocked? Here’s What to Know
snippet: You have a lot of options when buying a new iPhone. In this guide, we walk you through the decision process of exactly where to buy and whether to get an unlocked one.
fullText:
You might be planning to get a new iPhone, be it the rumored iPhone 18 Pro or the highly anticipated foldable iPhone Ultra. But besides choosing which phone to get, the next big question you might be pondering is “Where should I buy my phone?” Should you get it directly from Apple or through a carrier? 

Both methods have their pros and cons, and neither is best for everyone. Perhaps you like the idea of owning your phone outright without going through a third party. Or maybe you’d rather spread out your payments over time. Or perhaps you’re looking to upgrade your phone and switch carriers at the same time. Depending on your answer, you might prefer one path over the other. 

In this guide, we walk you through the process of deciding exactly where to buy your new iPhone, be it directly from Apple or through a wireless provider.

Buy directly from Apple

Apple will glady sell you its newest phone and revamped its Upgrade program to let people lease their next iPhone.Jeff Carlson/CNET

Since Apple makes the iPhone, it makes a lot of sense to simply buy the phone directly from the Apple Store. Though buying your iPhone from Apple is a common practice in a lot of countries, it’s not quite as popular here in the US due to the attractive financing options that wireless carriers offer. But buying your phone straight from Apple has its benefits. 

The primary reason to go through Apple is that you can buy the phone without being beholden to a wireless carrier. You have options. Instead of locking yourself down to one wireless carrier for multiple years, buying directly from Apple lets you get the phone completely unlocked.

Apple sells both unlocked iPhones and models tied to a specific carrier. The price is nearly the same, depending on which iPhone you get. But Apple drops the price by $30 when you buy and activate a new iPhone on a carrier at the time of purchase for models like the iPhone 17, which costs $829 unlocked or $799 after a carrier discount.

Unlocked models can be used with nearly any carrier you want, whether it’s a major carrier such as T-Mobile and AT&T or a smaller one such as Mint Mobile or Cricket Mobile. You can also swap out carriers every so often if you feel like it. While your iPhone may cost a pretty penny in the initial purchase, you could save on monthly bills in the long run, depending on your plan. 

Another strong reason to get an unlocked phone is if you travel a lot and want to use international travel eSIMs from companies such as Airalo or Saily. These eSIMs only work on unlocked phones. Otherwise, you’re stuck with your carrier’s international data plans, which are often a lot more expensive. 

If you don’t have the means to purchase the phone outright, you could opt for Apple’s Upgrade program, which lets you lease the phone through Klarna for 12 or 24 months. The phone will still be unlocked, but you’ll have to commit to one of the big three carriers: AT&T, T-Mobile or Verizon. 

Buy from a wireless provider

T-Mobile, Verizon and AT&T offer a variety of installment plans and trade-in deals on new iPhones.Joseph Maldonado/CNET

While there is a lot of freedom in buying an iPhone directly from Apple, it comes at a considerable cost. Even the most entry-level iPhone will cost you more than $600 upfront, while more premium handsets can easily cost over $1,000. On top of that, rising component costs could mean even higher prices going forward. It’s no wonder that so many Americans opt for carrier-based financing to purchase their phone. The iPhone 18 Pro could see a price hike, according to a Bloomberg report.

Not all carriers will offer financing, but the big three (AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon) certainly do. In addition to 12- and 24-month installments, some also offer financing up to 36 months, which is more than what Apple’s Upgrade program does. This can really help spread out your payments if you don’t mind sticking with one carrier for an extended period. 

Beyond just being able to pay over time, purchasing an iPhone through your wireless carrier has other benefits, too. Carriers like T-Mobile, for example, offer a 5-year price guarantee on future handsets, which is especially attractive in times of economic uncertainty. 

If you do plan to switch carriers when you buy a new phone, there are potentially even more incentives. Carriers often have new phone deals and could even offer financial assistance to pay off your current phone if you make the switch. There are also some that offer steep discounts if you trade in an existing phone. Sometimes, these incentives come in the form of bill credits, instead of an upfront discount or cashback.

Now that you have an idea about buying a new iPhone, check out our comprehensive guide to switching carriers if you’re looking for more insight on how to navigate the process.

title: Qualcomm’s upcoming premium chip has Adreno ‘Neural Fusion’ GPU
snippet: Following Qualcomm detailing the core Oryon CPU that would find itself on the next flagship Snapdragon chip, the chipmaker has announced its next-gen Adreno Neural Fusion GPU. more…
fullText:
Following Qualcomm detailing the core Oryon CPU that would find itself on the next flagship Snapdragon chip, the chipmaker has announced its next-gen Adreno Neural Fusion GPU.

Qualcomm’s next SoC will be the first chipset to feature dedicated AI GPU cores in the graphics pipeline. These so-called “Matrix Cores” sit snugly in each of the three 1.45GHz GPU slices on the new Adreno GPU. Qualcomm says they act as dedicated local hardware to “run advanced AI models directly inside the graphics pipeline.”

The Snapdragon chip’s Adreno GPU will also feature a dedicated 18MB HPM (High Performance Memory) cache. That capacity sounds humble, but Qualcomm says its HPM “provides large, low-latency memory directly to the GPU, allowing tile-based rendering,

frame buffers, and compute workloads to remain local to the graphics subsystem.”

Both components in the new core architecture help make up the entirety of the Adreno Neural Fusion GPU. For the end user, it means a 40% power improvement with the technology enabled. The company detailed in its press release how developing an SoC with AI processing done in closer proximity to the GPU means less latency and better efficiency.

	

The trick is keeping the work close to the silicon. Adreno Matrix Cores handle AI models right where the graphics happen, and the 18MB of Adreno High Performance Memory holds the heavy data—tiles, frame buffers, compute—on-chip so it isn’t constantly shuffling back and forth to system memory. Less movement means lower latency and better efficiency, which translates into gaming sessions that last longer.

For the time being, Unity and Unreal Engine have already integrated Qualcomm’s Neural Fusion stack.

The end result should be improved graphics quality with “upscaled images, stable frame rates, and improved efficiency through AI-enhanced rendering built directly into the Snapdragon

graphics pipeline,” as Qualcomm puts it.

Snapdragon Summit is scheduled for September 22-24, and more is set to be announced regarding the new chip’s NPU.

Adobe is bringing its creative and productivity tools directly into Slack, letting teams create and edit images, videos, designs and PDFs without leaving the conversations where projects already take shape.

Adobe says users can remove backgrounds and distractions, adjust lighting and tone, crop images and produce multiple variations from Slack.

Adobe for Slack is available globally to Slack Business+ and Enterprise+ customers across desktop, web and mobile starting today.

People can start without an Adobe account, while signing in unlocks more tools, generative AI features, Creative Cloud files and continuity across sessions.

The launch expands Adobe’s push to bring its tools into AI chatbots. Adobe already supports ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot, with Gemini integration coming soon.

title: John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO: Here’s the latest
snippet: Today is John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO. A new Bloomberg report has more details on other executive changes, plus tidbits on changes Ternus might make. more…
fullText:
Today is John Ternus’s first day as Apple CEO. A new Bloomberg report has more details on other executive changes, plus tidbits on changes Ternus might make.

Luca Maestri

Bloomberg reports that Luca Maestri is stepping down as Apple’s “Corporate Services” leader. Maestri served as Apple CFO until January 2025, when he stepped down to take on a smaller role. As head of Corporate Services, Maestri oversaw information systems and technology, information security, and real estate and development.

According to today’s report, Maestri left that job “in recent weeks.” He is, however, still on Apple’s payroll. His only remaining responsibility is “hosting a popular class at Apple University, an in-house program for teaching Apple’s ways to rising executives and employees.”

Bloomberg says that Maestri’s Corporate Services tasks have been shifted to CFO Kevan Parekh.

Adrian Perica

Mark Gurman points out that Apple’s new Leadership page excludes Adrian Perica, its head of mergers and acquisitions.

Apple’s new leadership page also excludes Adrian Perica, the company’s head of mergers and acquisitions. It remains unclear where he will shift within Apple. Bloomberg reported on Sunday that he would likely be dropped by Ternus as a direct report and could split his responsibilities across Apple’s services and finance teams.

It’s possible this signals a change to Apple’s strategy for mergers and acquisitions. Some analysts expect Ternus to be more aggressive in making bigger acquisitions.

A change to how Apple manages outgoing executives

Gurman also says that “people in and around Apple” expect Ternus to change how the company handles outgoing executives. While Cook made a habit of retaining executives in smaller roles, like Maestri, Gurman says “Ternus may be less likely to continue using this approach.”

More tidbits

Ternus officially joined X today, and his first tweet was an all-lowercase “hello” with no punctuation. The post was quoted by marketing exec Greg Joswiak, who wrote: “Hello, indeed. More to say September 9.”

Gurman says Apple is hosting an event at Apple Park today “to introduce John Ternus as its new CEO to employees and to again celebrate Tim Cook’s tenure.”

Laura Legros, a former Apple VP who Ternus recruited out of retirement last month, will reportedly serve in a “Chief of Staff” style role. Cook did not have a person like this around him, according to Gurman.

title: Meta launches Muse Voice Transcribe for real-time voice dictation on Mac
snippet: Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API. more…
fullText:
Meta is launching Muse Voice Transcribe, its first real-time audio perception model. It brings multilingual, streaming transcription to Meta AI for Mac, Muse Code, and developers through the Meta Model API.

Muse Voice Transcribe powers system-wide dictation on Mac

Meta Superintelligence Labs says Muse Voice Transcribe combines streaming automatic speech recognition with speaker diarization and endpointing.

In practical terms, it can transcribe speech as it happens, separate speakers across recordings with 20-plus voices, and determine when someone has finished talking, all without a separate post-processing step.

The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 validated at launch. It supports audio longer than an hour, plus native code-switching within or between sentences. Language, keyword, and context biasing can further improve recognition.

Rather than using one fixed tradeoff between speed and accuracy, Muse Voice Transcribe decides how long to listen before committing each word. Meta calls this “adaptive delay.” The system can move quickly through easier speech while using more audio context for difficult words.

Meta says the model ranks first on the Artificial Analysis streaming speech-to-text leaderboard as of September 1.

Muse Voice Transcribe is available today through the Meta Model API for $3 per 1,000 audio-minutes, equivalent to $0.18 per hour. 

It is also already powering dictation in Meta AI for Mac and Muse Code. On Mac, users can hold the Fn key to dictate into any application.

title: Sonos unveils ‘Sonos 27’ software with four new features
snippet: Today alongside launching two new products, Sonos has unveiled ‘Sonos 27’ branding for its software platform and detailed four new features coming soon for Sonos users. more…
fullText:
Today alongside launching two new products, Sonos has unveiled ‘Sonos 27’ branding for its software platform and detailed four new features coming soon for Sonos users.

Here are four new ‘Sonos 27’ features launching this fall

Sonos has launched Sonos Ace Ultra headphones today alongside a Sonos Beam Ultra soundbar. And in addition to the new hardware introductions, the company has rebranded its software.

‘Sonos 27’ is the official name of the Sonos software platform that already exists, but is getting a proper name starting today. More than just a rebrand though, Sonos announced four new software features coming this fall to Sonos users:

Portable surrounds

Personal listening

Sonos 27voice

Sonos MCP

Portable surrounds

Turn two compatible portable speakers into wireless rear surrounds for movie night — then move them right back to wherever they usually live when the credits roll. No wires, no permanent setup, no rearranging furniture.

Personal listening, without missing a beat

Headphone linking which is available in Early Access, allows you to seamlessly move audio between Sonos Ace Ultra and a compatible Sonos speaker or group streaming over the same WiFi connection with just the press of a button. title: YouTube overhauls its app-to-TV experience, shared Wi-Fi network no longer required
snippet: Casting from YouTube to your television has been a thing since, well, since Google first rolled out its Cast protocol well over a decade ago, and though the site’s default TV interface is pretty good these days, casting remains the preference of Chromecast veterans everywhere. If you count yourself among that crowd, good news: Google is overhauling how the app-to-TV experience works with YouTube. more…
fullText:
Casting from YouTube to your television has been a thing since, well, since Google first rolled out its Cast protocol well over a decade ago, and though the site’s default TV interface is pretty good these days, casting remains the preference of Chromecast veterans everywhere. If you count yourself among that crowd, good news: Google is overhauling how the app-to-TV experience works with YouTube.

As described in an announcement post on the YouTube support forums, Google is rolling out some big changes to how YouTube on your smartphone interacts with your television. The company is describing your device as a “companion” now, even ditching the classic Cast icon for something a little more generic. It’s a change that, based on Reddit threads, seemingly entered testing earlier in 2026, and is now ready for a full rollout. 

It’s not just a new way to describe pairing your devices, though. With this refresh, casting videos from your phone to a television now sounds like it has a whole lot less friction, thanks in part to a shift on completely relying on account-based management. These changes include:

No longer requiring both devices to be on a shared Wi-Fi network to cast. Instead, users will need to be signed in on the same account on both devices.

The ability to like videos, leave comments, and subscribe to channels while the video plays in the background.

The option to consume YouTube Shorts content on your phone while a different, full-length video plays on your television.

A built-in “Play on different device” option found within the menu button on every video listed in your homepage feed.

There are, of course, some caveats to these upgrades, and it primarily revolves around the shift to forcing account-based pairing between devices. While this should work wonders for private viewing sessions — i.e., casting a video from your own phone to your own television to watch either independently or with someone else in the room — it’s unclear if this completely removes the ability to cast over Wi-Fi, something that’s genuinely useful in larger gatherings with multiple participants. That’s a pretty common use case for watching YouTube on a television, so I’m hoping generic Cast support continues to exist in this format. Otherwise, this feels like a particularly anti-social change from Google.

	

Generally, though, these are all steps in the right direction, taking a lot of the existing Cast elements and simply streamlining them for a more modern second-screen experience. That “Play on different device” option, for example, appears to be pretty similar to the current casting menu, but won’t require you to begin playing a video on your phone prior to beaming it to your TV. Personally, browsing Shorts while watching a full-length video on your television sounds pretty overwhelming to me, but it’s certainly Google meeting modern viewers where they’re already at.

Today’s announcement did not include a specific rollout window, but it does sound like it’ll be coming to a mobile device near you very, very soon.

fullText:
In June, Anthropic first released Fable 5, its Mythos-class AI model for Claude. Three months later, Anthropic is enhancing Claude with its new Fable 5.1 model upgrade.

Claude Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 arrive today

In Anthropic’s world, Fable is Claude’s most capable model. Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus are the small, medium, and large models below Fable. 

“Claude Fable 5.1 sets a new standard on coding, knowledge work, and long-running problem-solving tasks,” Anthropic says. The company says the new model has a higher level of performance compared to Fable 5.

Anthropic also says Fable 5.1 “achieves similar or better results than Fable 5 at a much lower cost” when set to low or medium effort.

More from Anthropic below:

Fable 5.1 avoids shortcuts that result in poorer-quality work, and it’s smart enough to fix the root causes of software issues. For example, in testing by the investment firm Millennium, Fable 5.1 found the cause of a rare crash on their internal systems that none of their engineers (or any other model) had been able to explain after several years of trying.

In addition to Fable 5.1, Anthropic is also releasing Mythos 5.1 for users with Mythos access.

“Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1 are the same model, but with different levels of safeguards,” Anthropic explains. “Fable 5.1 is generally available, while Mythos 5.1 is available only through our trusted access programs; its safeguards are specifically designed to support work in cybersecurity and the life sciences.”

Here’s pricing data for Fable 5.1:

Fable 5.1 will cost an estimated 25% less than Fable 5 for typical workloads, wherever usage is billed by token. This is because we’re reducing our pricing on cache reads (where the model reads inputs that have already been processed and stored). For highly agentic work, the savings will often be much larger—up to approximately 45%.

In terms of pricing, Anthropic says it has “reduced the price of Fable 5.1’s cache reads (where the model reuses context it has already processed) wherever usage is billed by token, such as on our API.” The company says this “leads to a substantial reduction in the overall cost of running the model.” Pricing is otherwise unchanged from Fable 5.

title: Stoke Space raises another billion to rival SpaceX at re-flying rockets
snippet: Stoke has "completed the initial closing" of a $1B Series E round intended to help it reach orbit and prepare a new, larger rocket for operations.
fullText:
The fuel for a fully reusable rocket that can unlock truly low-cost access to space isn’t methane or liquid oxygen. It’s cash, and Stoke Space Technologies is tanking up. The company has now “completed the initial closing” of a $1 billion Series E round intended to help it reach orbit and prepare a new, larger rocket for operations.

“This round is really to scale,” CEO Andy Lapsa told TechCrunch. “To lay the infrastructure, to scale in production and flight frequency, and importantly to fund the development of the second generation vehicle.”

The round was led by Point72 Ventures (hedge fund billionaire Steve Cohen’s tech investment vehicle), and Spark Capital, and included investment from General Innovation, Glade Brook Capital, US Innovation Technology, Washington Harbour Partners, Woven Capital and Y Combinator, among others.

Stoke is one of a handful of startups attempting to compete with Elon Musk’s SpaceX in the low-cost rocket launch space. SpaceX was built around the Falcon 9, which has a reusable booster stage, and now Musk and company are trying to field a huge, fully-reusable rocket, Starship.

But unlike its rivals Rocket Lab, Relativity Space or Firefly Aerospace, Lapsa’s company is aiming straight at that holy grail: A rocket where both the booster stage and the payload-carrying second stage come back to Earth so they can be reused cheaply. It’s never been done before.

Such ambition and technical feats require capital. SpaceX has spent well over $10 billion on Starship over the last decade, and the vehicle still hasn’t yet reached orbit, although that may change on its next flight. Now, Stoke has raised $2.3 billion in total.

In particular, SpaceX has struggled to identify the right materials and configuration for the components that shield the second stage of the rocket from the extreme heat caused when it is reentering the atmosphere. Stoke instead flows super-cooled liquid hydrogen through its thermal shielding, a unique active cooling solution that Lapsa says has been tested exhaustively on the ground and will be deployed on the first flight.

“We can flow excess coolant — more than we think we need in order to overcool the surface of the vehicle — and take a conservative stance from that perspective in early flights,” he said.

Lapsa said that he expects Stoke’s first vehicle, the Nova Pathfinder, to take flight in early 2027. In a business known for delays, he’s confident sharing that target following a series of structural and operational tests on the rocket’s first stage at the company’s Moses Lake facility. Next up is test-firing each stage of the rocket on the ground to ensure they are ready for flight.

“The ground system is checked out to the extent that we can do it without the rocket, and the rocket’s checked out to the extent that we can do it without the launch pad,” Lapsa said. “So the next step is to do them together.”

The startup has already sold launch contracts on the vehicle, which can carry three metric tons to low-Earth orbit — that will be, Lapsa believes, the largest debut vehicle of any U.S. rocket maker. That said, few rockets get off the ground on time or with total success, and simply getting to orbit would be an achievement.

“We have multiple Pathfinder vehicles in production, and we have confidence that we will bring Pathfinder to market and into orbit regardless of this round,” Lapsa said.

Stoke also revealed plans for an even bigger rocket, the Nova Block 2, that has been under development for the past few years. Based on the same technologies as the Pathfinder, including the engines and the company’s novel heat shield, that vehicle will be able to bring 15 metric tons to low-Earth orbit, slightly more than the Falcon 9.

The goal is to deploy it in 2029, right when, according to Musk, the Falcon 9 will be phased out. Is Lapsa drooling at the possibility of picking up increasingly desperate launch customers just as SpaceX pulls back?

“It amplifies the mismatch between launch supply and demand for launch, there’s no question about that,” he admits. “Regardless of Falcon 9 retiring or not retiring, the space industry and the space economy scales exactly as fast as rockets get off the ground, particularly rockets that serve third-party customers.”

That last remark is a dog whistle that satellite operators will surely hear: When SpaceX’s Starship takes flight, companies and government agencies looking to buy tickets will be competing with the space company’s internal projects, and might have to pay a premium to use the big rocket. Stoke, on the other hand, has not revealed plans to operate its own space assets.

“Now is the time to get moving […] so that we can finally start deploying a lot of the constellations and applications that we aspire to as an industry but have been stuck on the ground,” Lapsa said.

He has closely covered the rise of the private space industry and is the author of  Rocket Billionaires: Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and the New Space Race. Formerly, he was a senior reporter at Quartz, the global business news site, for more than a decade, and began his career as a political reporter in Washington, D.C.

title: Apple invites developers to submit browser interoperability ideas for Interop 2027
snippet: Apple’s WebKit team is inviting developers to submit their ideas for Interop 2027, the next edition of the cross-browser initiative aimed at improving web interoperability. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple’s WebKit team is inviting developers to submit their ideas for Interop 2027, the next edition of the cross-browser initiative aimed at improving web interoperability. Here are the details.

A bit of context

Over the past few years, Apple has collaborated with Google, Microsoft, Mozilla, Bocoup, and Igalia on Interop, an annual effort to make modern web technologies work more consistently across different browsers.

The project began in 2022, building on the earlier Compat initiative, with participating browser makers and organizations identifying 15 key areas where interoperability issues were creating problems for web developers. While Compat was originally conceived as a one-off effort, it proved successful, and Interop has returned every year since.

Each year, the group selects a new set of focus areas, based in part on proposals from the web development community. Browser makers then work to improve their implementations in those areas, with progress measured through a shared set of Web Platform Tests.

Earlier this year, the WebKit team shared the results of Interop 2025, which saw the percentage of selected tests passing across all browsers jump from just 29% at the beginning of the year to 97% by the end.

They also outlined the 20 focus areas selected for Interop 2026, spanning CSS features and technologies such as the Navigation API, View Transitions, WebRTC, and WebTransport, partly based on proposals submitted by the web development community during last year’s open call.

Which brings us to this year’s open call, which officially opened on September 3 and will accept proposals through September 23.

Interop 2027 entries now open

Apple says that proposals must be based on mature web standards and be testable, since nascent technologies aren’t ready to become Interop Focus Areas, and the project relies on automated Web Platform Tests to measure progress across browsers. The company also notes that technologies that lack sufficient tests or testing infrastructure should instead be proposed as Interop Investigations.

Here’s what Apple says makes a “great” Interop 2027 proposal:

The best submissions are typically:

Specific: Identify a specific interoperability issue. One feature (or narrow group of related features) per proposal. Think font-size-adjust, not “typography”.

Impactful: Provide a clear description of the interoperability problem that needs addressing. Use cases from your own experience are especially helpful.

Valuable: Explain how web developers and/or users will benefit. Why is this more valuable than other existing options? Is there evidence this is a common need (perhaps survey results)?

Stable: Link to the stable web standard that defines the technology you want improved. (Find it on the MDN web doc for that technology. Like here.)

Tested: Look up and link to WPT test coverage. If more tests are needed, how can they be created this fall?

Read the Interop Proposers Guide to learn more.

The company also notes that developers should be mindful that not everyone reading this year’s proposals will have full knowledge of last year’s proposals, and that they must “take the time needed to fully make” their case.

That includes explaining why the proposed focus area is important, how the current state of affairs affects web developers and users, how widely the technology is used, and why addressing the issue should be a priority over other potential focus areas.

Developers can submit their own proposals by filing an issue on GitHub, or support an existing proposal by adding comments that help strengthen its case. Apple says it is better to contribute to an existing issue than to submit multiple proposals covering the same or very similar ideas.

To learn more about Apple’s guidelines and recommendations for submitting an Interop 2027 proposal, follow this link.

title: We need to talk about Siri AI for Apple Watch
snippet: Siri AI on Apple Watch arrived two cycles late for watchOS 27 beta this summer. I had high hopes for how new Siri could transform Apple Watch into an AI wearable. What actually happened in July and August is that Siri has been remarkably unusable in watchOS 27 beta. Like “hold off on updating” bad. This week, I half-expected Apple to remove “Siri AI” from watchOS 27 beta 8 and revert to the previous version of Siri. Instead, I think Siri AI on Apple Watch actually got good? more…
fullText:
Siri AI on Apple Watch arrived two cycles late for watchOS 27 beta this summer. I had high hopes for how new Siri could transform Apple Watch into an AI wearable.

What actually happened in July and August is that Siri has been remarkably unusable in watchOS 27 beta. Like “hold off on updating” bad.

This week, I half-expected Apple to remove “Siri AI” from watchOS 27 beta 8 and revert to the previous version of Siri. Instead, I think Siri AI on Apple Watch actually got good?

Siri AI on Apple Watch has been a major regression this summer

The issues that plagued Siri AI on Apple Watch all summer were clear.

Siri has been slow and unresponsive. At times, Siri has been unable to do tasks like set alarms and create reminders.

Setting a timer while cooking? Go ahead and subtract at least 30 seconds from the timer to give Siri time to get it together.

Controlling HomeKit accessories with Siri on Apple Watch has also been terribly slow with watchOS 27 beta. Really, just any normal Siri task on Apple Watch: starting a workout, sending a text, you name it.

Based on two months of pre-release betas without signs of improvement, I thought Apple might need to delay Siri AI on Apple Watch. At least for existing hardware… or maybe they were just going to mess up Siri for everyone who updates? 

watchOS 27 beta 8 appears to shape things up just in time

Well, it’s been a few days since watchOS 27 beta 8 arrived, and I think all of my summer beta issues with Siri AI are just fixed now.

	

I’m always cautious to declare something resolved that could still be an issue for others. But at least in my experience, it’s a night-and-day difference with Siri AI on Apple Watch this week. I hope that’s true for everyone.

I’ve really enjoyed Siri AI for easily getting answers to the kind of knowledge questions that my curious 8-year-old son asks me. It’s especially great to do this without needing my phone. AI on Apple Watch has been a pretty big gap for the last couple of years, and Siri AI solves it — as long as it actually works.

I’m optimistic for the first time since Siri AI arrived in beta that it actually does work now. Are you testing Siri AI on Apple Watch yet? How has your experience been this summer and this week? 

(Now my one watchOS 27 complaint is that double-clicking the Digital Crown no longer jumps between recent apps… maybe watchOS 27.1 will do something with the double-click gesture. For a device so button-constrained that only the Ultra gets an Action button, it’s odd to see a double-click gesture replaced with … nothing.)

title: LG TVs caught spying even when offline or on standby
snippet: The LG G5 OLED is one of the TVs tested by Gamers Nexus. | Photo by John Higgins / The Verge LG smart TVs are almost constantly logging and uploading data about owners and their homes, even when offline or on standby mode, according to a new report from YouTube channel Gamers Nexus. The company's TV sets scan Wi-Fi networks for nearby devices, record audio logs through their microphones, and use audio and video sampling to recognize exactly what you're watching from across the TV inputs. Gamers Nexus partnered with fellow YouTubers Level1Techs and independent security researchers for the investigation, which involved testing retail LG OLEDs. Packet captures showed the TVs scanning the local area network for nearby hardware like pho … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Dominic Preston

 

is a news editor with over a decade’s experience in journalism. He previously worked at Android Police and Tech Advisor.

LG smart TVs are almost constantly logging and uploading data about owners and their homes, even when offline or on standby mode, according to a new report from YouTube channel Gamers Nexus. The company’s TV sets scan Wi-Fi networks for nearby devices, record audio logs through their microphones, and use audio and video sampling to recognize exactly what you’re watching from across the TV inputs.

Gamers Nexus partnered with fellow YouTubers Level1Techs and independent security researchers for the investigation, which involved testing retail LG OLEDs. Packet captures showed the TVs scanning the local area network for nearby hardware like phones or smartwatches, as well as logging location data and details of nearby Wi-Fi networks, and feeding the information back to LG Ad Solutions. Perhaps more concerningly, the TVs were capable of recording microphone audio when in standby; this continued even after the TV was disconnected from the internet, with audio files stored offline and uploaded once a connection was restored.

The final piece of the puzzle is Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), tech that uses audio and video data to figure out what you’re actually watching, examining the apps you use through the TV’s own smart interface and the content you connect via HDMI and other ports. ACR isn’t just an LG issue though: A new video from RTINGS digs into how ACR is used by almost every smart TV manufacturer to figure out what you watch.

This isn’t LG’s first brush with Gamers Nexus. In July this year, the channel flagged that some LG monitors were automatically installing an app that collected device data and ran pop-up ads for LG’s other apps and even McAfee antivirus. The public pressure from that video prompted an intervention from Microsoft, and ultimately led to LG disabling the pop-up ads.

title: Apple faces yet another lawsuit over App Tracking Transparency, with a twist [U]
snippet: While Apple has long used privacy as a selling point for both its hardware and services, I do wonder whether it now regrets introducing one privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT). For something with rather limited scope, it sometimes feels like scarcely a month goes by without a new antitrust lawsuit or regulator challenging it. A third ATT lawsuit is being brought in the UK – this one with a twist. This piece has been updated with a response by Apple at the end of the piece … more…
fullText:
While Apple has long used privacy as a selling point for both its hardware and services, I do wonder whether it now regrets introducing one privacy measure: App Tracking Transparency (ATT).

For something with rather limited scope, it sometimes feels like scarcely a month goes by without a new antitrust lawsuit or regulator challenging it. A third ATT lawsuit is being brought in the UK – this one with a twist.

This piece has been updated with a response by Apple at the end of the piece …

Personalized advertising has been one of the hot button tech topics for many years now. Instead of seeing random ads for products that may or may not interest us, we are shown ads based on our interests, as gleaned from the apps we use and the websites we visit.

In theory, this is a win for all parties. Consumers are shown ads that may genuinely interest them; advertisers get better results from their ad spend because it is targeted; while free apps and websites funded by ads get higher payments for the same reason.

Although the data used to serve personalised ads is collected in an anonymised form, the practice has led to a widespread perception of it as an invasion of privacy. Even when Apple specifically developed a technology to ensure that this data was anonymous, many consumers remained suspicious.

App Tracking Transparency

Apple’s App Tracking Transparency was designed to solve the problem by letting consumers choose whether or not their data could be used to serve personalized ads. Developers who wish to collect this data must ask consumers for permission.

Unfortunately for the iPhone maker, this has led to a whole slew of lawsuits and antitrust investigations, mostly based around the fact that Apple’s own apps don’t seek this permission. The company has on numerous occasions pointed out that its rules are in fact consistent: Apple’s own apps don’t present the ATT prompt because they don’t collect the data it references. Third-party apps that don’t collect this data are also exempted from the need to present the prompt.

The latest UK lawsuit

Apple has so far faced three complaints to the UK’s relevant antitrust regulator, the Competition Appeal Tribunal. Apple lost the first of these – though is currently appealing – and the second one is still ongoing.

Reuters reports on the third, which was filed today.

Apple is facing a £2 billion ($2.7 billion) London lawsuit brought on behalf of app developers over its app tracking rules, with the ​iPhone maker accused of abusing its power to unfairly impose ‌greater restrictions on third parties. The lawsuit, filed at London’s Competition Appeal Tribunal on Thursday, follows years of regulatory scrutiny over Apple’s App Tracking Transparency feature.

With a twist

The latest lawsuit has an interesting twist: it’s being brought by Ann Pope, who was previously a senior official with the regulator behind today’s case.

Ann Pope, a former senior official with Britain’s Competition and Markets Authority who ​is leading the lawsuit, said Apple’s policy “resulted in very significant harm ​to businesses that depend on Apple as a gatekeeper”.

“This action is important to protect ‌the ⁠rights of British businesses that depend on Apple, to ensure that the rules that Apple applies are fair, and to compensate the losses that British companies have suffered,” Pope said in a statement.

Apple recently agreed to make eight changes to its ATT rules in the EU following an investigation by the German antitrust regulator. In respect of this lawsuit, the company told us:

At Apple, we believe privacy is a fundamental human right, and we created App Tracking Transparency to give users a simple way to control whether apps have permission to track their activity across other companies’ apps and websites. Apple is bound by the exact same requirements as all developers under ATT, and this feature has been embraced by our customers and praised by privacy advocates and data protection authorities around the world, including in the UK. We disagree with these claims, and will continue to defend strong privacy protections for our users.

A number of privacy advocates have spoken up in support of ATT over the years.

title: Ford explains why it chose Apple Maps over Google for its new EVs
snippet: Earlier this year, Apple announced a partnership with Ford to bring native Apple Maps integration to the automaker’s upcoming Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) Platform, including what we now know is called the Fathom. more…
fullText:
Earlier this year, Apple announced a partnership with Ford to bring native Apple Maps integration to the automaker’s upcoming Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) Platform, including what we now know is called the Fathom.

In a new interview, Alan Clarke, Ford’s vice president of advanced vehicle projects, elaborated on the decision to use Apple Maps instead of Google Maps and what this means for CarPlay Ultra.

In an interview with GreenCars, Clarke said Ford spoke with Apple, Google, and others about mapping for the Fathom. Ultimately, the company turned to Apple:

“We had to optimize for performance capabilities cost, quality, you name it. We spent time determining which was the best solution.

A couple of things about Apple Maps.

One is that it has gotten so much better over the last few years. It’s a really great solution. The team that we worked with at Apple was very flexible to ensure that we get the absolute best customer experience.”

Clarke said Ford wanted a close working relationship with the Apple Maps team. There are a lot of factors that go into mapping for an EV, including things like range, charger availability, weather, and more. Taking all of those things into account, Ford determined Apple offers “the best solution.” 

“We wanted to make sure that we had really tight integration with that team when we’re talking about the things that have to happen on a vehicle: range estimation and determining how much range you have and how you want to precondition the batteries and how you charge.

You need a great maps provider that has the capability to get elevation, weather, and the maps data to have accurate updated information about chargers.

I think we thought that Apple was the best solution for this vehicle in order to get the customer the best solution.

It’s amazing to be first as well. Apple Maps looks beautiful, and having a large display to be able to put it on we think will be a really big wow factor for our customers when they get to see it.”

Clarke also confirmed that this is Ford integrating Apple Maps into its native, in-car software platform. The automaker is not adopting CarPlay Ultra in the Fathom. Instead, it will offer native Apple Maps, plus standard CarPlay and Android Auto.

With CarPlay support, Ford drivers can choose between Apple Maps, Google Maps, Waze, and other mapping solutions. They can also easily access many excellent third-party CarPlay apps.

title: How Tim Cook shaped Apple’s foldable iPhone, and what it may cost
snippet: On the eve of Apple’s special event, Bloomberg is out with a new report detailing the decade-long foldable iPhone development. The report highlights former Apple CEO Tim Cook’s involvement in the project. Plus, details on how much the foldable iPhone could cost. more…
fullText:
On the eve of Apple’s special event, Bloomberg is out with a new report detailing the decade-long foldable iPhone development. 

The report highlights former Apple CEO Tim Cook’s involvement in the project. Plus, details on how much the foldable iPhone could cost. 

Mark Gurman says Apple engineers started iPhone Fold development around 2016. In 2020, Cook returned home from a trip to China and was “unusually energized” about foldable phones. He reportedly pushed Apple’s hardware teams to accelerate work on the company’s first foldable. 

Typically, Cook “stayed away from the conception of new products.” Therefore, his involvement in the foldable iPhone’s development gave the project added weight:

Cook’s enthusiasm helped change the direction of the work to something that could be more mainstream. Rather than begin with a foldable iPad, Apple turned its focus to creating a foldable iPhone. “Tim was the earliest and biggest champion of this,” one of the people said. “He saw them everywhere in Asia and said Apple needed to play in this space.”

In terms of pricing for the foldable iPhone, which everyone inside Apple refers to as the iPhone Ultra, the company originally targeted an entry-level price of $1,999. Most recently, however, rising component costs have shifted that goal to $2,199. 

More recently, Apple has discussed pricing the foldable product as high as $2,199, according to one of the people, who said various options have been considered in recent weeks and that the memory shortage has led Apple to blow past its cost goals.

Some larger-storage configurations of the device could approach $3,000. Compare that with the standard iPhone, which currently starts at $799, or the iPhone 17 Pro, which begins at $1,099.

Apple is expected to debut the iPhone Ultra tomorrow. 9to5Mac will be inside Steve Jobs Theater to cover everything in depth.

fullText:
When shopping for an electric vehicle, affordability is becoming a more common trait. But affordable and energy efficient is truly a rare breed. Often you have to sacrifice one for the other. Want something affordable? Great, here’s a range loser. Want something that goes the distance? Be ready to pay the price.

Surprisingly, here comes Audi to split the difference. The German automaker’s new A2 E-tron compact crossover is inexpensive, starting at just £32,200 (about $45,000). And it absolutely impresses with an ultra low drag coefficient and a range of battery and drivetrain options that, when configured correctly, can produce a range of up to 401 miles.

Unfortunately for us Yanks, this rear-wheel drive compact car is just for the European market for now. But perhaps Audi will eventually see the error of its ways, or Americans will get their heads out of their tailpipes long enough to see the real advantages of a highly efficient, compact EV with an Audi badge.

1/6

Efficient is often synonymous with aerodynamic, and the A2 E-tron certainly confirms that. Flush door handles, cool air intakes, a fully enclosed underbody, and gap reducers around the wheel arches help reduce the drag coefficient down to 0.24, a first for Audi. Another first is bidirectional charging, which will help support vehicle-to-load via an outlet in the trunk, or vehicle-to-home with the right compatible DC wall box.

With the right motor and battery setup, the A2 E-tron consumes just 12.8 kWh per 62 miles (100 km), while the real mile-eater of the lineup manages up to 401 miles (645 km) on the European WLTP cycle. Inside, the A2 E-tron features a standard curved MMI panoramic display that combines an 11.9 inch digital gauge cluster with a 12.8 inch center touch screen.

1/7

There’s also plenty of clever storage thanks to a Fidlock magnetic fastening system that allows owners to click things like cupholders and charging cable bags into dedicated points around the cabin and trunk. Cyclists may be familiar with the tech that can keep their water bottles attached to their bike without a cage, but Audi says this is the first time it’s making an appearance in a production car.

While Audi gave up on its EVs-or-bust pledge last year, the automaker is leaving the door open for a mix of gas, hybrid, and electrification. The A2 may not be appearing alongside its brethren like the impressive S6 Sportback E-tron at the dealership anytime soon, but nothing is set in stone.

title: WhatsApp for Android loophole lets private photos be accessed without unlocking
snippet: A loophole in WhatsApp for Android lets someone see private photos on your device without the device being unlocked, which obviously isn’t supposed to happen. more…
fullText:
A loophole in WhatsApp for Android lets someone see private photos on your device without the device being unlocked, which obviously isn’t supposed to happen. 

First spotted by @VBarraquito on Twitter/X and further confirmed by “Mobile Hacker” and NotebookCheck, a very straightforward flaw exists within WhatsApp for Android that allows someone to access a user’s private photos before the device is unlocked. 

This works by first having a WhatsApp call pop up and be answered – this doesn’t require the phone to be unlocked, just like a standard phone call – at which point the user can tap a button to use filters and effects on their video feed, including Meta’s AI to edit a photo – you can see where this is going. Instead of preventing access to photos, the preview is shown clearly before the phone ever asks to be unlocked with a PIN or biometrics.

This isn’t universal, though. NotebookCheck found that a Galaxy device does force the lockscreen to be unlocked before reaching this step, while Pixel and Oppo devices both allowed the full bypass. The loophole doesn’t exist on iPhone, where WhatsApp is forced to use the native iOS calling UI.

	

The plastic piece here has nothing to do with the exploit, and is presumably only for covering a contact name

The good news: this doesn’t seem to bypass the lockscreen fully, as accessing any other part of the device is still blocked. There’s also not much that can be done with the photos beyond physically seeing them – though a malicious party could use this to take photos of those images with a second device. 

WhatsApp should be able to patch this with an update, but no such update has been announced at this time. The loophole has been reported to both WhatsApp and Google. 

In the meantime, a temporary workaround is to set WhatsApp’s photo/video access to “limited” in Android’s permissions, which breaks the loophole.

title: Philips Hue adds HDMI-free Sync and new 4K Box, Nanoleaf integration, and more app upgrades
snippet: To kick off IFA 2026, Philips Hue announced a new set of sync boxes for its Play lighting. The company also teased a few new app long-awaited changes to the app, and a Nanoleaf partnership that makes your light-up triangles compatible with Philips Hue’s products. more…
fullText:
To kick off IFA 2026, Philips Hue announced a new set of sync boxes for its Play lighting. The company also teased a few new app long-awaited changes to the app, and a Nanoleaf partnership that makes your light-up triangles compatible with Philips Hue’s products.

Philips Hue’s Play Sync Box 8K is an incredible addition to any home theater or living room, but it’s expensive. At around $385, you can connect your TV’s visuals with compatible Philips Hue lights, but that isn’t a feasible option for a lot of users.

Camera-based light kits have become popular for users who want the experience without spending the money on Philips’ good-but-pricey hardware. Options from companies like Govee fill that gap for much less.

Today, though, Philips Hue announced that it’s going to offer a couple of more affordable options for users, starting with its own camera-based sync box. The Philips Hue Play Screen Sync is made up of a single fisheye camera that sits on the top of your TV. It captures colors displayed by your TV, so not only is it more affordable, but it’s input-agnostic. Unlike the 8K Sync Box, this model will work with native TV apps because it isn’t pulling from select HDMI feeds.

	

The Philips Hue Play HDMI Sync Box 4K sits in the middle of three, with a similar experience and compatibility to the higher resolution version. It only has one HDMI connection, which might make it ideal for those that just need a connection to an AVR, instead of media players and consoles.

Both new models can also opt to sync to devices through Bluetooth instead of using a Hue Bridge. That makes the setup simpler. The Hue Bridge and Hue Bridge Pro allow connections to expand to 10 lights, as opposed to a single light strip.

With that, new gradient strip lights were announced for entertainment spaces. Philips Hue says these strips will be available for TVs up to 100 inches.

The IFA announcement continues with an announcement regarding a new partnership with Nanoleaf. The company says compatible Nanoleaf shapes can be integrated into the Philips Hue ecosystem with the Wall Light Module. Those devices will work with Hue’s scenes and automations within app control.

The app itself is also getting a couple of changes. First, Philips Hue on Android and iOS will get backup and restore functionality, so users don’t lose their scenes and automations if the app is deleted or they switch phones. The app will also introduce Custom AI Behaviors, which use natural-language instructions to create more sophisticated and personalized automations by combining triggers, conditions, and lighting actions.

Both of those upgrades will roll out “beginning in fall 2026.”

The new Philips Hue Play Screen Sync will start at $119, while the Play HDMI sync box will be available for $149. Both are now available on Philips Hue’s website and retailers like Amazon.
