title: This New 360 Camera Won’t Come to the US. I Went to Berlin to Test It
snippet: Replaceable lenses, new image sensors and 8K60 video. The hardware of the DJI Osmo 360 II is not the problem.
fullText:
I traveled all the way to Berlin to test out DJI’s new 360 camera. OK, not just for that, but it was definitely one of the reasons. You see, due to the ongoing FCC block on new DJI products by the US government, it’s likely the new Osmo 360 II won’t be available in the US. Which is too bad because, as was the case with this camera’s predecessor, the hardware is top-tier.

The 360 II improves on the older Osmo 360 with new image sensors, dual, square 1-inch image sensors, as well as a maximum resolution and frame rate of 8K60. It bests Insta360’s X6, which maxes out at 8K50. Those 10 extra frames per second might not seem like a big deal, but in many situations, they can be the difference between having usable footage and not. Probably the biggest improvement, however, is the addition of user-replaceable lenses.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

Unfortunately, the prospect of availability in the US through official channels is gray. As gray as the market where you’ll inevitably find this camera. With fingers crossed for future US availability, DJI loaned me a 360 II for a few days in Berlin to check it out.

The Osmo 360 II’s hardware is too different

On the outside, the second-gen model is similar to its predecessor. There are some exposed screwheads that give it a slightly tougher look, but the screen and buttons remain the same. There’s also a larger mic opening on the front. 

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The most notable change is the switch to user-replaceable lenses. As someone who’s used and ruined numerous 360 cameras over the years, I’d advise you not to overlook this feature. It’s all too easy to accidentally scratch a 360-degree camera lens since they stick out from the body. Repairs, when possible, can be costly, too. So being able to replace them yourself should be considered a must-have “feature” for most people. 

The rest of the images in this story are from the Osmo 360 II and been reframed or cropped but otherwise unedited.Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The other major change is new, square, 1-inch sensors. DJI says these have 14.5-stops of dynamic range. I didn’t get a chance to do much low-light testing, but it seemed solid. The earlier 360 was already good in this regard. 

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

Thanks to these new sensors, better processing or both, the Osmo 360 II is capable of 8K60 video. This bests Insta360’s flagship X6, which maxes out at 8K50. For most people, this isn’t a big deal. Most phones can’t edit 8K video, and for social media, the lower 6K-resolution video is plenty unless you want to zoom in. 

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

That said, in the US, our displays are on multiples of 30 or 60. So 50 doesn’t work as well, potentially leading to stuttering movement or strobing background lights. Also, for more advanced users who can edit 8K, the extra resolution will help with more flexible framing and cropping options. If those same pros are recording sports or other fast movement, 60fps is far better than 30. Which is to say, for most people, 8K60 versus 8K50 isn’t a big deal, but for certain people, it will be a very big deal.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

Despite this being a “first look” and not a full review, there are a few features found on other 360 cameras I wish the Osmo 360 II had. Being able to select the aspect ratio for single-lens photos would be great. Sure, you can do this in the editing process, but seeing your frame ahead of time helps, as does one less thing to edit later. Similarly, there are limited options to change the field of view with single-lens photos; the option is merely cropping in and reducing resolution if you don’t want an ultrawide, almost fisheye FOV. The X6 can double as a regular, wide-angle camera far more easily with these features.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The software

As with other DJI gear, the hardware isn’t the problem. You’ll need to download the DJI Mimo app from DJI directly on Android phones and disable some security settings. Not ideal. It is available on Apple’s App Store, so that’s one less issue if you’re on iOS. The app itself works well, letting you crop and edit photos and videos. There aren’t quite as many options here as there are on Insta360’s app, but it’s also not as bloated.

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

Full circle (well, sphere)

Competition is important. Insta360 is the biggest name in the 360 camera space, but with GoPro’s future uncertain and Kandao’s output slowing, we on the consumer side need Insta360 to have a big competitor to keep driving 360 camera development. While the X6’s 8K50 isn’t a huge deal for most people, it’s interesting that a camera released mere months later can do 8K60 just fine. I have no doubt that a future X7 will have 8K60, so why this interim step? 

Geoffrey Morrison/CNET

The geopolitics of DJI in the US is far above my pay grade to write about. For now, it’s making getting this interesting camera overly difficult. If it does get approved for sale in the US, or is at least reasonably easy to get, we’ll give it a full review. For now, I guess we’ll have to wait and see.

Dinner in Berlin with the CNET/ZD crew.Geoffrey Morrison/CNET
excerpt:
I traveled all the way to Berlin to test out DJI’s new 360 camera. OK, not just for that, but it was definitely one of the reasons. You see, due to the ongoing FCC block on new DJI products by the US government, it’s likely the new Osmo 360 II won’t be available in the US. Which is too bad because, as was the case with this camera’s predecessor, the hardware is top-tier.

The 360 II improves on the older Osmo 360 with new image sensors, dual, square 1-inch image sensors, as well as a maximum resolution and frame rate of 8K60. It bests Insta360’s X6, which maxes out at 8K50. Those 10 extra frames per second might not seem like a big deal, but in many situations, they can be the difference between having usable footage and not. Probably the biggest improvement, however, is the addition of user-replaceable lenses.

title: Apple will quickly become a dominant player in folding phones – Counterpoint
snippet: Counterpoint Research has predicted that global foldable phone shipments will surpass 100 million units by the end of this year, with the iPhone Ultra playing a major role in this growth. fullText:
Counterpoint Research has predicted that global foldable phone shipments will surpass 100 million units by the end of this year, with the iPhone Ultra playing a major role in this growth. The firm says it expects Apple to take 25% of the entire market this year – and it may be the biggest player by the same time next year.

In timing unlikely to be coincidental, the Xiaomi 18 Fold, leaked last month, is officially launching in China the day before Apple’s event …

iPhone Ultra set to have a major impact

While folding smartphones get a lot of attention, Counterpoint says that they currently only account for about 2% of the total market. This is expected to change significantly in the next 12 months, with 24% growth expected this year and a further 37% next.

The report says the market will see new products from Samsung, Apple, Huawei, Motorola, Honor, Google, Vivo, Oppo, and Xiaomi. The firm says Apple will be entering the market with a bang.

Apple’s entry will likely make an immediate impact. Counterpoint forecasts up to 6 million foldable iPhone shipments in 2026, giving Apple a 25% share of the global market and the No. 2 position, behind Samsung at 38% and ahead of Huawei at 22%.

It will be significant for Apple to achieve this ranking so quickly after entering the category, particularly given the relatively short selling window expected this year […] A full year of Apple sales will be a major driver, with Apple shipments expected to more than double and its share set to reach 40%.

That would exceed Samsung’s current 38% share.

Xiaomi launches 18 Fold on eve of Apple event

Xiaomi, which has made a name for itself by cloning many Apple products, appears to be seeking to do the same with its 18 Fold. 

The upcoming model, which shares the book format of the iPhone Ultra, which was leaked toward the end of last month before being shown off at IFA, has now officially launched on the eve of Apple’s Surprise and Shine event.

title: New iPhone 18 Pro report details flagship camera feature and more
snippet: iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will be unveiled next week, and a new report offers fresh details on the flagship “mechanical aperture” camera feature that’s coming, plus mentions an improved vapor chamber and more. more…
fullText:
iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will be unveiled next week, and a new report offers fresh details on the flagship “mechanical aperture” camera feature that’s coming, plus mentions an improved vapor chamber and more.

Here’s what’s coming with iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, per Mark Gurman

Today Mark Gurman at Bloomberg published his latest expectations for the new iPhones being introduced on September 9.

While most of the report covers features reported previously, a few noteworthy details stand out.

For example, Apple has a new “mechanical aperture” camera feature coming to iPhone 18 Pro Max—and possibly the smaller iPhone 18 Pro too.

Despite plenty of reporting on this camera upgrade, which has also been called “variable aperture,” there have been minimal details on what it will enable. But Gurman reports today that it will be “for fine-tuning light adjustments and depth control.”

Additionally, the new report says iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max will have “better battery life and improved vapor chambers to prevent overheating.”

Battery improvements were already expected, but good to see confirmed. The mention of improved vapor chambers is a new detail, though.

Apple first debuted a vapor chamber in the iPhone last year with iPhone 17 Pro. It seems the company already has a second-generation version ready to go.

Finally, Gurman says “in-house C2 modems” are coming to iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max. While this isn’t a new rumor, it’s worth highlighting because some reports have claimed Apple is sticking with Qualcomm modems again this year.

For more on what to expect from iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, see our coverage here.

title: This Android phone has a detachable action camera, coming to the US for $999
snippet: IFA 2026 is delivering a pretty wild new Android phone that’s not only rugged, but has a GoPro-like action camera built-in which can be detached and used for capturing footage on the fly. more…
fullText:
IFA 2026 is delivering a pretty wild new Android phone that’s not only rugged, but has a GoPro-like action camera built-in which can be detached and used for capturing footage on the fly.

The RugOne XSnap 7 Pro first appeared earlier this year, but is now making a splash with official pricing and release information at IFA. The device is landing on Kickstarter next week and will cost $999 when it arrives in the US in October – €1,099 in Europe.

This rugged device comes from Ulephone, a known brand for these ruggedized Android smartphones, with “RugOne” being a new sub-brand under the company. And, as per usual, it’s a chonky device with a 19.1mm profile, IP68/IP69K/MIL-STD-810H certifications, and no need for a case with its rugged, drop-resistant design. It has a 6.67-inch FHD+ display using Gorilla Glass Victus on top, runs on a MediaTek Dimensity 8400 chip with 12GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, and has a massive 9,300 mAh battery. It even has a 64MP night vision camera to back up its 50MP main sensor. 

But the claim to fame here is a built-in, detachable action camera.

	

The camera attaches to the phone magnetically with a 133-degree field-of-view and 2.7K (1440p) recording. It can record for 40 minutes on its built-in battery and has 64GB of storage for up to eight hours of storage, but a built-in app on the phone can let the camera use the phone’s storage to offload that footage, and the phone also recharges the camera. The app can let you stream from the camera from up to 50 meters away and the action camera is waterproof up to 5 meters with no additional equipment.

It’s a wild idea, and one that actually seems more compelling than most of these rugged devices. A clear bit of utility, decent specs, and even a promise of software support – it XSnap 7 Pro ships with Android 16 and is promised updates through Android 20. 

What do you think?

title: Galaxy Z Fold 8 has been fully restocked as trade-ins plummet; Fold 8 Ultra drops to $1,799
snippet: Samsung has fully restocked its smash-hit Galaxy Z Fold 8 while also discounting the usually-more-expensive Galaxy Z Fold 8 UItra. more…
fullText:
Samsung has fully restocked its smash-hit Galaxy Z Fold 8 while also discounting the usually-more-expensive Galaxy Z Fold 8 UItra.

Following some early stock shortages and a behind-the-scenes scramble to make more units, Samsung has fully restocked the Galaxy Z Fold 8 in the US. The wider foldable is currently available across every color and storage variant on Samsung.com, something that wasn’t the case even a couple of days ago. All variants are also shipping in two weeks or less, with most reporting shipping dates as early as next Tuesday.

Galaxy Z Fold 8 at Samsung.com

Samsung has dropped trade-in offers by a fair bit, now capping trade-in credits at $800 compared to $1,200 during the pre-order window, but it’s still not all that hard to get a good deal on a Fold 8.

Even more so the Fold 8 Ultra, which Samsung has officially discounted across all channels. Samsung.com, Best Buy, Amazon, and more have all cut the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s starting price from the usual $2,099 down to $1,799, a clear signal that the company’s former form factor isn’t resonating as much this year. The steep discount also makes the Ultra device cheaper than the wide Galaxy Z Fold 8. 

	

While Samsung shows the lower price on its main dashboard, it’s not showing for all users. There is a $350 instant savings credit available if you skip a trade-in, though, which cuts the price to $1,749. Galaxy Z Flip 8 is also down to $1,049 right now.

title: Apple tells Mac App Store developers they can now drop Intel support
snippet: Apple started informing developers today that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now drop support for Intel-based Macs. more…
fullText:
Apple started informing developers today that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now drop support for Intel-based Macs.

In the email, Apple says:

We’re reaching out to let you know that universal macOS apps on the Mac App Store that require macOS 13 or later can now remove support for Intel-based Mac computers.

By removing support for Intel-based Mac computers, you can simplify your development and optimize your download and on-device size.

To remove Intel support, update your app build settings to “arm64” only. Then rebuild and submit your app to the Mac App Store.

Previously, developers were required to offer Intel compatibility. With today’s change, developers can drop support for Intel-based Macs. Intel users, however, can continue using the last version of the app compatible with their machine.

The changes come as macOS 27 Golden Gate drops support for Intel-powered Macs altogether. Apple also announced last year that Rosetta 2, the software that translates Intel apps for Apple Silicon, will be discontinued after macOS 27 (with some exceptions for for certain games).

fullText:
Apple won the ‘Best Picture’ Oscar for CODA back in 2022, and now director Siân Heder is back with another potential winner: Being Heumann. Here’s the new trailer.

Being Heumann gets first trailer ahead of November release

Apple TV just added a lot of classic movies to its library, and the streamer has a packed lineup of original films coming soon too.

One standout title is Being Heumann, from director Siân Heder. Heder’s last project was CODA, which won Best Picture at the Academy Awards. With that win, Apple TV became the first streaming service to win the top Oscar—beating out Netflix.

Being Heumann will stream November 13 on Apple TV following a limited theatrical bow one week prior.

The company clearly hopes for similar success with Being Heumann, and the film’s newly released trailer positions it as an awards contender.

Here’s the plot summary followed by the trailer:

They wouldn’t take Judy Heumann’s phone calls, so she took their building. In 1977, a young disabled woman (Ruth Madeley) and a scrappy coalition of outsiders decide they’ve had enough. What begins as one impulsive act becomes the longest occupation of a federal building in American history, as hundreds spontaneously seize government offices and refuse to leave until the bureaucrat in their way (Mark Ruffalo) takes action. Bringing rebellion in all its forms to the hallowed halls, a movement’s accidental leaders struggle to find their path forward where none has ever been paved for them. Directed by Academy Award winner Siân Heder (“CODA”) and based on true events, “Being Heumann” is the revolutionary, irreverent and deeply human story of the least likely people trying to pull off the impossible and change the lives of millions.

Other noteworthy films coming to Apple TV soon include Ryan Reynolds’ Mayday, which premieres later this week, John Cena’s Matchbox the Movie, fellow Oscar contender Tenzing, and more.

title: What we expect from the upcoming Apple launch
snippet: While Apple's first foldable iPhone Ultra will headline the September 9 launch, we're also expecting news about AirPods and HomePods.
fullText:
It’s finally happening — this week, we are (probably) about to see Apple’s first foldable iPhone, more than five years after Samsung launched its first foldable phone.

Apple’s annual iPhone release events are always interesting in one way or another, but this year’s presentation is one of the most anticipated in a while. As Tim Cook hands off the CEO role to former Vice President of Hardware Engineering John Ternus, people have high expectations for Apple’s next devices, especially since the company is embracing an entirely new form factor.

While Apple is usually tight-lipped about its product launches, there are always inevitable leaks, giving us insight into what we might see during the September 9 Apple event. While the foldable iPhone is most exciting, we’re also anticipating news about AirPods, HomePods, and the non-foldable iPhone 18 line. 

What we think we know so far about the foldable “iPhone Ultra”

If Apple has made its consumers wait over half a decade for it to enter the foldable market, its first attempt had better be good — especially since reports indicate that the phone will cost more than $2,000. At least it’s not as pricey as the $3,500 Apple Vision Pro headset, and unlike headsets, people actually buy smartphones.

The good news is that people who claim to be early testers of the device have reported back positive experiences. According to Bloomberg’s Apple insider Mark Gurman, the foldable iPhone has a premium feel, fits nicely into a pocket, and opens up into a wide, iPad-like display. The phone is expected to sport a 5.5″ cover display, which expands to 7.8″ when the screen is unfolded. When folded in, the device will look shorter and wider than a typical iPhone.

To make hardware that’s still sleek enough to pocket when folded, Apple has had to make some concessions. The device reportedly skips the telephoto camera, which could be disappointing to the kind of consumers who are willing to open their pockets for a phone that’s expensive enough to feed a family for months. However, the phone is expected to have a dual-lens rear camera system with a main and an ultra-wide lens, similar to what’s on Apple’s more basic iPhones.

Rumor has it that Apple will include MagSafe, the magnetic wireless charging and accessory system, but that it will forego Face ID to save space, relying instead on a Touch ID fingerprint button on the phone’s side. This shouldn’t be a huge concession — touching a button is about as easy as looking at a screen — but it might take some getting used to if you’ve become accustomed to Face ID.

Like other foldable phones, the iPhone Ultra is expected to support side-by-side multitasking, letting you run two apps at once, one on each half of the unfolded screen. Even though it’ll resemble a small iPad when opened up, it will still run iOS rather than iPadOS, though shouldn’t be cause for concern, since Apple’s newest chips are powerful enough to handle it. In fact, the same chip reportedly powers Apple’s budget MacBook Neo laptop.

A pain point for foldable phone users thus far has been the dreaded “crease.” With other companies’ foldable phones, you can see the evidence when you open the phone that this isn’t your standard display. It’s a hard problem to solve and one that maybe isn’t worth the technical effort, though Apple has supposedly created a display where the crease isn’t as visible.

Don’t worry, you can still get a new iPhone that doesn’t fold

If foldables aren’t your thing — or if you don’t want to spend double the price on your next phone — don’t worry. Apple is also expected to release some new devices in the iPhone 18 line. We’ve heard leaks about the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, but not much yet about the standard iPhone 18, which is predicted to arrive six months after the September event. That would be a first for Apple — releasing the premium models before the standard one.

Siri HomePods? AirPods with cameras? 

Now that Apple is finally moving forward with its Gemini-powered Siri AI update, the company is also expected to refresh the HomePod, a smart speaker and Apple’s answer to devices like the Amazon Echo line. 

References to unreleased products, including new HomePods, were recently spotted by users digging through a macOS preview build.

The most surprising find, however, is that Apple appears to be working on AirPods with built-in cameras. In that same macOS preview, researcher Aaron Perris found a video showing someone wearing the AirPods and picking up a book.

“With Visual Intelligence, your world becomes savable. See something you like? Just ask me to save it for later,” a voiceover in the video says.

While some users may be skittish about using a device that can see what they see — comparisons to Meta’s maligned “pervert glasses” are inevitable —  we have some degree of hope that a company like Apple, which has built its brand on privacy, will do better.

Gurman has reported that “the cameras essentially act as eyes for the Siri digital assistant and aren’t designed to take photos or video.” Instead, the earbuds’ components allow it to “capture visual information in low resolution.”

Amanda Silberling is a senior writer at TechCrunch covering the intersection of technology and culture. She has also written for publications like Polygon, MTV, the Kenyon Review, NPR, and Business Insider. She is the co-host of Wow If True, a podcast about internet culture, with science fiction author Isabel J. Kim. Prior to joining TechCrunch, she worked as a grassroots organizer, museum educator, and film festival coordinator. She holds a B.A. in English from the University of Pennsylvania and served as a Princeton in Asia Fellow in Laos.

fullText:
As the debut of Googlebook quietly approaches, a week full of new laptop launches at IFA continues to make me wonder why literally anyone should be even a tiny bit interested in Google’s new platform.

This issue of 9to5Google Weekender is a part of our newsletter that highlights the biggest Google stories with added commentary and more. Sign up here to get Weekender delivered to your inbox every weekend, and catch our weekday roundups too!

Googlebook made its debut earlier this year as the company’s Android-based desktop platform that will replace ChromeOS and, frankly, I’ve spent the last couple of months just sitting here stewing over the complete lack of information on what this platform is supposed to do and why anyone should care. Truly, I cannot remember the last time I was this skeptical about a Google product – is this how other people felt about Stadia?

At this point, not much has changed.

	

We’ve seen leaks of some of the first Googlebook laptops from Asus and Lenovo, while Acer was spotted teasing its Googlebook at IFA in Berlin. Some early apps have shown up too, including “Magic Pointer” which is the one new feature Google has actually shown off from this platform, a “Desktop Camera” app, and “Look up” which is in fact not a reference to that DiCaprio movie but instead an AI-powered experience that lets you interact with text to find relevant information such as definitions, flight tracking, and more. That one works on some Android phones, too. 

Yet, I still cannot fathom where Googlebooks fit into the larger market. ChromeOS had a clear selling point – stable and usable software on low-cost hardware, with later generations adding in some clever AI features and using more capable hardware. But where Googlebook might have been interesting from a cost perspective, a focus on “premium” hardware combined with RAMageddon and a sea of MacBook Neo competitors… I just don’t get it folks. 

The new IdeaPad Vibe from Lenovo and the Dell 14S were both announced this week as direct answers to Apple’s hit budget-conscious laptop, and Google is literally going in the opposite direction.

Damien laid out some potential ideas back in June, such as a focus on AI-aided vibe coding, but it’s still hard to imagine Google’s pitch at this point. Windows laptops are getting more affordable in the wake of the MacBook Neo, and is anyone looking to spend money on tech they don’t need to right now? Maybe I’m just having trouble seeing the potential or the positives here, but I can’t remember the last time I was so sour on a potential new Google launch. 

What do you think?

title: M6 MacBook Pro: Three new upgrades launching this fall
snippet: Apple has a new M6 MacBook Pro launching this fall with a 14-inch screen and the current industrial design. Now that the M6 chip has officially been unveiled, here are three upgrades to expect from the new MacBook Pro. more…
fullText:
Apple has a new M6 MacBook Pro launching this fall with a 14-inch screen and the current industrial design. Now that the M6 chip has officially been unveiled, here are three upgrades to expect from the new MacBook Pro.

#1: Dual 16-core Neural Engine

If AI is in any way significant to your workflows—and with macOS 27, it will be for even more users—then the M6 MacBook Pro could be a big upgrade.

That’s because the M6 chip includes a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, up from the standard 16-core version available in M5 and prior. Per Apple:

M6 also introduces a Dual 16-core Neural Engine, providing up to 2x the peak compute over previous generations to make on-device AI workflows run even faster. System frameworks can automatically utilize both engines simultaneously, enabling applications to see faster model execution.

#2: 12-core CPU and GPU with powerful new cores

The base M6 chip offers a 12-core CPU and 12-core GPU. Both are solid upgrades over the M5, which was limited to 10 cores each.

M6’s new CPU cores are especially interesting, as Apple is bringing three distinct core types to its base chip for the first time. It has 2 super cores, 4 performance cores, and 6 efficiency cores. Here’s what Apple says about each core:

Super cores: “blaze through single-threaded workloads”

Performance cores: “use less power and join the super cores to run demanding multithreaded workloads”

Efficiency cores: “handle everyday background tasks”

Previously only M5 Pro and M5 Max—and now M5 Ultra—provided super cores and performance cores in a single chip. But now these Pro-level capabilities are available for standard M6 users. 

#3: Major efficiency gains to likely improve battery life

M6 is the first Apple chip built on a new 2nm process. And the company says that brings the benefit of “a major leap in performance and power efficiency.”

Currently the only product with an M6 is the new Mac mini, which doesn’t run on a battery.

But in the MacBook Pro, MacBook Air, and other upcoming M6 products, the new chip’s “major leap” in power efficiency is likely to enable longer battery life.

Apple could always opt to shrink the physical battery to offer comparable performance as before, but here’s hoping it uses M6’s improved efficiency to deliver better battery life instead.

title: Apple has reportedly canceled innovative product that was ‘Ternus priority’
snippet: A new Omdia research note today outlined Apple’s reported Mac and iPad roadmap for the years ahead, and it also mentioned that a key rumored product has been canceled. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
A new Omdia research note today outlined Apple’s reported Mac and iPad roadmap for the years ahead, and it also mentioned that a key rumored product has been canceled. Here are the details.

Foldable iPad/Mac hybrid that was John Ternus ‘priority’ has reportedly been canceled

For years, rumors have suggested that the iPhone will be just the first Apple product line to adopt foldable displays.

Reporting suggests that a larger, roughly 18- or 20-inch foldable iPad/Mac hybrid device has been in the works for years. At one point it was believed to be coming as early as 2026 before later being pushed to 2028.

Earlier this year, Mark Gurman called the product a “Ternus priority” but also suggested it may never launch. He wrote:

Apple has been working on a roughly 20-inch foldable iPad. This device has been a Ternus priority but may end up being a wacky experiment that doesn’t see the light of day, according to several people who have worked on it.

You can find a good overview of prior rumors about the product here.

According to today’s Omdia report, it seems Gurman’s suspicions may have been right. It says: “product plans for 16.1-inch to 18-inch foldable MacBooks have been canceled.”

Based on prior rumors, this seems to be the same product previously covered by Gurman and others.

	

It’s very possible Apple is taking a “wait and see” approach with this foldable product as it gauges reception to the foldable iPhone Ultra. If iPhone Ultra is a hit, maybe the company will accelerate development of the iPad/MacBook hybrid.

But perhaps with the current memory crisis causing product pricing to rise so significantly already, Apple doesn’t see a current path forward for an ultra-premium, innovative foldable device like this.

title: Hikers rescued after using Google Gemini for planning
snippet: The sheriff’s office said the hikers “were advised by Gemini to bring far less food and water than their group required."
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

12:35 PM PDT · September 5, 2026

Image Credits:Christian Richards / EyeEm / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Three hikers were rescued from California’s Mount Shasta this week after using Google’s AI chatbot Gemini to plan their expedition, according to the Chicago Tribune.

A report from the Siskiyou County sheriff’s office said that three young men set off on their hike at 3 a.m. and that even though hikers are told to turn around if they haven’t reached the summit by noon, they made it to the top at 7 p.m. 

The trio then tried to descend in the dark, called the sheriff’s office to ask for directions, and spent the night in Mud Creek Canyon before being rescued the next morning by Forest Service rangers and volunteers.

While it’s not clear whether Gemini can take all the blame for these bad decisions, the sheriff’s office said the hikers “were advised by Gemini to bring far less food and water than their group required, especially when their planned 8-hour ascent became a multiday ordeal.”

“It is always advisable to call the local USFS Mount Shasta ranger station ahead of your trip to ensure you have the most accurate information, and to never rely solely on AI for your trip planning,” the sheriff’s office said.

title: Sony Surprises With New 1000XM4C 2nd Gen Headphones With Updated Sound, Bluetooth 6.0
snippet: The $300 WH-1000XM4C will be released alongside Sony’s new midrange CH730N and entry-level CH530 headphones.
fullText:
When Sony’s WH-1000XM4 headphones hit the market back in August 2020, I awarded them a CNET Editors’ Choice Award, calling them nearly flawless. Despite their age and the release of two successors — the WH-1000XM5 and WH-1000XM6 headphones — the 1000XM4s remain quite popular.

Now, Sony is leaning into that legacy model’s popularity with the new WH-1000XM4C (M4 2nd Gen), which comes in new color options and has “updated sound tuning designed for today’s listening preferences,” according to Sony. The WH-1000XM4C headphones list for $300 and are being launched alongside the new WH-CH730N ($180) and WH-CH530 ($80).

Read more: Best Headphones of 2026

WH-1000XM4C’s small differences

Aside from some tiny cosmetic changes, the M4 2nd Gen headphones look identical to their predecessor. The XM4C’s most notable feature upgrade is Bluetooth 6.0 instead of Bluetooth 5.1, and the headphones now support a new 10-band equalizer (and gaming EQ) for “greater sound personalization,” instead of the older five-band equalizer.

The WH-1000XM4C comes in three color options, including a new lavender color that will only be available online at Sony and Amazon. Sony says the XM4 has been popular among younger female users, and the new color is targeted at them.  David Carnoy/CNET

The 1000XM4C (M4 2nd Gen) are still equipped with Sony’s QN1 chip along with four microphones (the WH-1000XM6 have 12 by comparison), so their noise-canceling performance is the same. Battery life has dipped a bit: The M4 2nd Gen are rated for up to 27 hours with noise canceling on, compared to the original’s 30 hours.

The original M4 headphones were known for having strong, dynamic bass and a slightly warmer sound profile than their successors. The foundation of that profile remains, but the new tuning helps deliver cleaner, more refined sound overall.

WH-CH730N is a true second-gen midrange model

I was fond of Sony’s over-ear CH-720N headphones because they were lightweight and comfortable while sounding good and offering decent noise-canceling performance for a reasonable price. (They listed for $150 but dipped to as low as $100 during flash sales.) While the list price for the new WH-CH730N has gone up $30 to $180, the model offers a similar value proposition in a new foldable design, along with improved performance all around. Plus, they promise better battery life at up to 50 hours with noise canceling on, according to Sony.

The WH-CH730N comes in white, pink, blue, black and a new oat color. David Carnoy/CNET

I like the new design, which looks and feels slightly more premium than their predecessor’s, and the headphones are quite comfortable. The new headphones’ sound is slightly improved, too. They lack the clarity and depth that you get with Sony’s more premium headphone offerings, but the sound is open and well-balanced with some nice warmth to it (the bass goes pretty deep, too). They’re pleasant headphones to listen to.

While the noise canceling certainly isn’t up to the level of what you get with Sony’s flagship WH-1000XM6, it has been upgraded with Sony’s Dual Noise Sensor technology and is pretty decent (Sony says it’s about 10% more effective). The bigger performance gain is arguably with the voice-calling performance, as the headphones have beamforming microphones with optimized microphone placement and AI noise reduction.

They, too, have a 10-band equalizer with a gaming EQ setting. And while they don’t support Sony’s advanced LDAC audio codec, they do support the LC3 audio codec, which is new (they support SBC and AAC). Alas, like their predecessor, while they come with a cable for wired listening, they do not come with a carry pouch or case.  

The WH-CH730 in their new oat color on the left.David Carnoy/CNET

Entry-level on-ear WH-CH530 get small upgrades but cost more

Sony’s earlier CH-520 was a pretty basic on-ear model that didn’t have noise canceling, but sounded good for its relatively low price (the headphonea list for $60 but were often discounted to less than $50 and sometimes as low as $38, as they are now). Available in new color options, the new WH-CH520 list for $20 more and offer some small upgrades — most notably, improved voice-calling performance with AI noise reduction. However, they don’t seem like a true next-gen product like the CH-730N.

The CH-530 headphones are available in cobalt, coral, mint, pink, white and black.David Carnoy/CNET

The headphones are targeted at younger folks and now have a volume limiter feature, which should appeal to parents with young kids. Their battery life is rated at up to 55 hours. They don’t support wired listening, so you can’t plug them into an in-flight entertainment system. Nor do they come with a carrying pouch or case.

Priced for discounts

List prices for headphones have been creeping up, but all of Sony’s new so-called “value” models should see decent discounts heading into the holiday shopping season. The 1000XM5 headphones are currently selling at $198 at Amazon as part of a limited-time deal, so there’s no reason the M4 2nd Gen shouldn’t hit something close to that price in the not-so-distant future. Also, take the $180 price on the CH-730N with a grain of salt, as that model should see $50 discounts in flash sales, particularly around Black Friday.

I just received review samples of all three models, and I’ll have full reviews of the M4 2nd Gen and WH-CH730N later this month, including comparisons of their performance.

fullText:
Like other Google apps, Messages for Android A/B tests many features. It can take the RCS/SMS client a rather long time to actually launch new functionality in stable. From various reports, Google announcements, and devices we’ve checked, this is the current state of Messages.

Update 9/7:

Still rolling out (beta)

These are Messages features that Google announced or have been spotted in the wild by beta users.

Customizable attachments grid

Google is testing two designs, with the one on the right taking up more of your screen.

	

Learn more

Instead of a top toolbar, long-pressing on a message or image opens a floating menu as the background blurs. Another press lets you copy just a part of the chat. Previously, you had to copy the entire message.

Learn more

iOS 27 adds replies & photo reactions to Android-iPhone RCS

When iOS 27 launches this fall, Android-iPhone conversations over RCS will gain support for inline replies that include quotes, as well as photo reactions with the actual emoji instead of just the text description. This feature is currently in beta.

More

Read receipts redesign II

In recent weeks, Google Messages has mostly reverted to the two-circle read receipts underneath the message design after trying a single circle within the bubble.

Google is now testing a variant that uses the old icons but moves the timestamp and encryption lock. You now view that information by swiping left, with direct replies accessed by a right swipe.

Learn more

Messages for web removing QR code pairing

Going forward, Messages for web users will have to use Google Account sign-in. As of late April, the QR code method is still available.

Learn more

Read receipts redesign I

Read receipts are now placed in a circle at the bottom-right corner of message bubbles and images. You swipe left to see timestamps and the encryption lock, while you can swipe right to reply. This first started appearing in August of 2024, but is now seeing wide beta and stable availability.

title: Samsung is shutting down ‘Quick Measure’ and ‘AR Doodle’ apps for Galaxy phones
snippet: Samsung is shutting down two long-available augmented reality (AR) apps on Galaxy phones, with “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” both going away later this year. more…
fullText:
Samsung is shutting down two long-available augmented reality (AR) apps on Galaxy phones, with “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” both going away later this year.

Confirmed in Galaxy Store listings for both the “Quick Measure” and “AR Doodle” apps, Samsung will be shutting down these AR experiences on December 31, 2026. Samsung explains that both will be “returning with improved services in the future.”

“Quick Measure” is an AR app that lets you get measurements of real-world distance from your phone, while “AR Doodle” lets you “draw” on real-world locations through the camera app.

The shutdown will block new downloads of both apps, while also pulling the plug on any future updates. The app won’t just stop working immediately, but any OS updates will break the apps in time. Notably, Samsung seems to have hidden both app listings on the latest One UI versions, making them inivisible in the Galaxy Store.

	

Samsung says:

Please be advised that service for the Quick measure app is scheduled to be terminated on 31 December 2026.

After this date, new downloads and update support for the existing app will be discontinued. You may continue to use the app if it is already downloaded, but please be aware that some features may not function properly.

Additionally, compatibility support for the Quick measure app will no longer be provided for future OS updates.

We apologise for any inconvenience this may cause and thank all our customers for their loyal use of the Quick measure app. We are committed to returning with improved services in the future.

It’s unclear when these replacement apps might arrive, but it’s certainly a shame to see these going away.

title: Google Messages slowly rolling out fix for bug that randomly sends old texts to other people
snippet: A bug in Google Messages is causing the app to randomly send old text messages to other random people and, while it’s still happening, a fix is slowly on the way. more…
fullText:
A bug in Google Messages is causing the app to randomly send old text messages to other random people and, while it’s still happening, a fix is slowly on the way.

The issue at play here sees Google Messages reviving old messages that were sent to a contact and sending those alongside another new message to a different contact. You can see the problem, right? A message meant for your significant other could theoretically be sent to your parents, for example. It’s been reported by many users in recent weeks, with the problem even visible in real time; some have tested sending themselves messages only to see old messages randomly inserted into the same thread.

Highlighted by Droid-Life, there are still reports of this behavior popping up right now, with some reports popping up just in the past day.

It’s not happening for everyone, but it’s obviously a major issue for those affected. Sending old messages to random people could, at the very least, result in confusion, but could go as far as revealing private information. 

	

In a statement, Google confirmed that it is aware of the issue and has a fix, but it’s not rolling out quickly. Google said:

We’re currently rolling out a fix that will reach everyone over the coming weeks. Please ensure you stay up to date with the most recent version of Google Messages.

That was on September 2, and reports continue to pop up now, the better part of a week later. Updates continue to land on Google Play, so go check for a patch if you’re affected. Let us know in the comments below if you’re running into this bug.

title: Apple TV’s big fall lineup: Here’s every new show and movie coming soon
snippet: Apple TV is now airing Ted Lasso season 4, and more high-profile shows and movies are coming to the streamer soon. Here’s everything in Apple TV’s fall lineup so far, which could keep growing as more premieres are announced. more…
fullText:
Apple TV is now airing Ted Lasso season 4, and more high-profile shows and movies are coming to the streamer soon. Here’s everything in Apple TV’s fall lineup so far, which could keep growing as more premieres are announced.

September

Mayday

When: September 4

What: Movie

Genre: Action-Comedy

Ryan Reynolds and Kenneth Branagh team up in “Mayday,” a genre-bending, action-packed buddy comedy that flips the spy thriller on its head. When hotshot U.S. Navy pilot Lieutenant Troy “Assassin” Kelly (Reynolds) is sent on a top-secret mission into Russian territory at the height of the Cold War, the operation implodes, leaving him stranded behind enemy lines. Discovered by Nikolai Ustinov (Branagh), a gruff ex-KGB agent with a penchant for American culture, Troy thinks he’s toast — but could an unlikely alliance between the two lead to Troy’s rescue and a bond neither saw coming?

Watch Mayday here on Apple TV

Last Seen

When: September 9

What: TV Show

Genre: Thriller

Police detective Ian Ridley’s (Patrick Brammall) life fell apart 11 years ago when his young daughter, Maggie, disappeared without a trace. Now working as a police dispatcher, the only thing that has kept him going is his implacable refusal to accept that she might be gone forever. When he receives a distress call from a teenage girl he is certain is Maggie, he will stop at nothing to find her and reunite his broken family, whatever the cost.

Slow Horses (season 6)

When: September 16

What: TV Show

Genre: Espionage Thriller

This darkly funny espionage drama follows a team of British intelligence agents who serve in a dumping ground department of MI5 due to their career-ending mistakes. Led by their brilliant but irascible leader, the notorious Jackson Lamb (Academy Award winner Sir Gary Oldman), they navigate the espionage world’s smoke and mirrors to defend England from sinister forces.

Brothers

When: September 23

What: TV Show

Genre: Comedy

“Brothers” follows McConaughey and Harrelson, who play fictionalized versions of themselves, and whose lifelong friendship is thrown into chaos when they uncover a decades-old secret: they might actually be brothers. After Woody’s daughter’s wedding falls apart, he loads up the family and heads to Austin for an extended stay at Matthew’s ranch. But what begins as a healing getaway quickly spirals when Matthew’s mother, Ma Mac (played by Holland Taylor), accidentally lets slip a long-buried secret that the two friends might actually be brothers. As Woody turns the ranch upside down in pursuit of the truth, Matthew finds himself juggling an entirely different identity crisis: a potential run for Governor of Texas. The result is a heartfelt, chaotic and wildly funny story about friendship, family, fame and the messy line between myth and reality.

October

The Last First: Winter K2

When: October 2

What: Movie

Genre: Documentary

In “The Last First: Winter K2,” Amir Bar-Lev tells a complex, harrowing and moving story that unpacks the industry of extreme mountain climbing and its changing culture. Focusing on a 2021 expedition, mountaineers John Snorri Sigurjónsson, an Icelander, and the Pakistani father-son team of Ali and Sajid Sadpara set out to be the first to summit K2 in the winter, when the mountain’s conditions are the cruelest. The men soon find themselves sharing the treacherous ascent with influencer climbers and their film crews, commercial expedition clients and Nims, a Nepalese celebrity mountaineer, and his team of Sherpas. “The Last First: Winter K2” takes us to the icy heights and unpredictable weather of K2 and reveals a surprising and layered story — one of strategy and determination, class and caste, money and power — all under life and death circumstances.

The Sisters Grimm (season 2)

When: October 2

What: TV Show

Genre: Kids & Family

Two orphaned sisters navigate a town full of people torn straight from fantasy and fairy tales, confronting heroes and villains alike, while investigating the mystery of their missing parents. “The Sisters Grimm” blends discovery, fantasy and adventure to deliver important lessons for all ages.

Small Prophets

When: October 7

What: TV Show

Genre: Comedy

“Small Prophets” is a comic tale of the eccentric Michael Sleep (Pearce Quigley) who, since his darling Clea disappeared seven years ago, has lived a very ordinary life. He works in a DIY store, visits his dad Brian (Sir Michael Palin) and hopes for Clea to return. One day Brian shares an old recipe involving rainwater, horse manure and more than a little alchemy. With recipe in hand, Michael sets out (albeit with some skepticism) to create homunculi — magical spirits that can predict the future — in the hope they have the answer to his burning question: “will I ever see Clea again?”

Matchbox The Movie

When: October 9

What: Movie

Genre: Action

Inspired by the iconic Mattel toys, “Matchbox The Movie” is an action-packed, globetrotting adventure about a group of friends since childhood who have their lives upended when undercover CIA agent Sean (John Cena), their long-absent former leader, returns to their small town and unwittingly gets them embroiled in a frantic international pursuit to save the world.

Tenzing

When: October 16

What: Movie

Genre: Drama

Based on true events, “Tenzing” chronicles the little-known story of Tenzing Norgay (Genden Phuntsok), a gifted Himalayan climber who, alongside New Zealand mountaineer Edmund Hillary (Tom Hiddleston), was the first to summit Mount Everest. Encouraged by his wife Dawa (Thinley Lhamo), Tenzing finds an ally in expedition secretary Jill Henderson (Caitríona Balfe). Together, they persuade Colonel John Hunt (Willem Dafoe) that Tenzing belongs on the British climbing team, rather than merely serving it. Where Western climbers see “Everest” as something to be conquered, Tenzing reveres “Chomolungma” as the sacred mother goddess. What follows is an ascent defined as much by the tensions between backgrounds, classes and competing ambitions as by the perils of the mountain itself. But high above the world, empire, rank and aspiration fall away, leaving two outsiders bound by mutual respect and trust — and for Tenzing, the fulfillment of both a lifelong dream and a spiritual calling.

Where’s Wanda? (season 2)

When: October 21

What: TV Show

Genre: Dark Comedy

Apple’s first German-language series “Where’s Wanda?” is a dark comedy that tells the story of Dedo and Carlotta Klatt, who are desperate to locate their missing 17-year-old daughter Wanda, who disappeared months ago without a trace. When the police fail to find her, the family takes matters into their own hands, obtaining surveillance devices with the help of their tech-savvy son Ole. Disguising themselves as employees of an electrical company, they bug their neighborhood and then half their suburb, finding out that behind closed doors, none of their neighbors are who they pretend to be.

Nocturne

When: October 30

What: TV Show

Genre: Crime Drama

The series tells the story of Jonah Lynn (Liev Schreiber), an ex-soldier turned homicide detective who, tired of working the tough streets of Philadelphia, moves to a small town in western Pennsylvania for a quiet life. But, as the town and his family come under attack from the diabolically cunning serial killer Jurek Walter (Graham), Jonah must protect all that he holds dear. When the desperate search for Jurek’s last missing victim forces Jonah to send his surrogate daughter, FBI Agent Saga Bauer (Beetz), up against Jurek, how far will Jonah go?

November

Stick (season 2)

When: November 4

What: TV Show

Genre: Comedy

“Stick” is a sports comedy series created by Jason Keller and starring and executive produced by Owen Wilson. Wilson stars as Pryce Cahill, an over-the-hill, ex-pro golfer whose career was derailed prematurely 20 years ago. After the collapse of his marriage and while working at an Indiana sporting goods store, Pryce hedges his bets, and future, entirely on a troubled 17-year-old golf phenom named Santi (Peter Dager). “Stick” is a heartfelt, feel-good comedy about a found family and their relationships set within the world of golf as it has never been shown before.

12 12 12

When: November 13

What: TV Show

Genre: Heist Drama

Each episode of “12 12 12” unfolds across three timelines of a heist: the 12 months of planning, the 12 hours of the heist and the 12 days following it. The series follows a disgraced FBI agent (Anthony Mackie) and an American career criminal (Jamie Dornan) as they play a zero-sum game of cat and mouse across Europe. At the center of it all is the daring, epic raid on a bank vault deep beneath the streets of Zurich.

Being Heumann

When: November 13

What: Movie

Genre: Drama

They wouldn’t take Judy Heumann’s phone calls, so she took their building. In 1977, a young disabled woman (Ruth Madeley) and a scrappy coalition of outsiders decide they’ve had enough. What begins as one impulsive act becomes the longest occupation of a federal building in American history, as hundreds spontaneously seize government offices and refuse to leave until the bureaucrat in their way (Mark Ruffalo) takes action. Bringing rebellion in all its forms to the hallowed halls, a movement’s accidental leaders struggle to find their path forward where none has ever been paved for them. Directed by Academy Award winner Siân Heder (“CODA”) and based on true events, “Being Heumann” is the revolutionary, irreverent and deeply human story of the least likely people trying to pull off the impossible and change the lives of millions.

Way of the Warrior Kid

When: November 25

What: Movie

Genre: Action-Drama

Middle school has been a nightmare for Marc (Jude Hill), a good kid who’s bullied by his classmates and feels like he’s behind in everything, from academics to P.E. to just making friends. That changes when his injured Uncle Jake (Chris Pratt), a decorated Navy SEAL, comes to spend the summer and recuperate with Marc and his mom, Sarah (Linda Cardellini). To help Marc defend himself, Jake devises an ambitious program he calls “Operation Warrior Kid” based on his SEAL training. Instead of teaching his nephew how to fight, Jake shows Marc what real courage is, facing down his own demons along the way. Based on the bestselling novel by former Navy SEAL Jocko Willink, “Way of the Warrior Kid” is directed by McG (“Charlie’s Angels,” “Terminator Salvation”) from a screenplay by Will Staples (“Without Remorse,” “The Right Stuff”).

title: Read John Ternus’s full memo to Apple employees on his first day as CEO
snippet: New Apple CEO John Ternus has just sent his first company-wide memo. In it, Ternus thanks Tim Cook and recognizes that Apple is “so lucky to have had a CEO who led with his values and with such decency and humanity.” “We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal,” Ternus also says, in reference to Apple’s forthcoming “Surprise and shine” special event. Read the full memo, obtained by 9to5Mac, below. more…
fullText:
New Apple CEO John Ternus has just sent his first company-wide memo. In it, Ternus thanks Tim Cook and recognizes that Apple is “so lucky to have had a CEO who led with his values and with such decency and humanity.”

“We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal,” Ternus also says, in reference to Apple’s forthcoming “Surprise and shine” special event.

Read the full memo, obtained by 9to5Mac, below. 

Ternus also looks further ahead in message, teasing the “incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet.”

Here is the full memo from Ternus sent to Apple employees today. 

Team,

Today, on my first day as CEO, I just wanted to send a quick note to thank everyone for the warm wishes. I also want to extend my deep appreciation to Tim for sharing so much of his knowledge and experience during this transition, and more importantly, for everything he contributed to Apple over the years. We’re so lucky to have had a CEO who led with his values and with such decency and humanity. We are all better for it, and I’m so grateful he’ll be our executive chairman.

I’m honored to be stepping into this role at what is truly the greatest company in the world, and I am so excited about everything we have in store. We have a huge launch next week that’s going to be phenomenal. Thanks for everything you’ve all done to make it possible.

I’m just as excited about what lies beyond that, including the incredible products already in the works and the ones we haven’t even imagined yet that we’ll dream up and create together. There’s no team in the world I’d rather build the future with.

More to come. In the meantime, thanks for your excellent work!

John

title: Dell’s new 14S laptop exists to challenge MacBook Neo and, somehow, might be even cheaper
snippet: Apple’s MacBook Neo has made waves in the laptop world because it’s a remarkably well-built and reliable laptop at a very affordable price – though one that’s a bit higher now thanks to RAMageddon. Dell is ready to challenge that with its new Dell 14S laptop announced at IFA, and it somehow might be even cheaper. more…
fullText:
Apple’s MacBook Neo has made waves in the laptop world because it’s a remarkably well-built and reliable laptop at a very affordable price – though one that’s a bit higher now thanks to RAMageddon. Dell is ready to challenge that with its new Dell 14S laptop announced at IFA, and it somehow might be even cheaper.

The Dell 14S is directly positioned as an “affordable” laptop for “students, college, and everyday life.” It features an aluminum build, 21 hours of battery life, and either an Intel Core Ultra 3 or Core Ultra 5 processor. The 16:10 display has 60Hz and 120Hz options while the hardware has two USB-C ports and an HDMI port, as well as a headphone jack. 

Dell says the 14S weighs in at around 2.5lbs and is just 13.5mm thick. 

In a Q&A on its blog, Dell directly positions the 14S as a “compelling” alternative to the MacBook Neo, though pricing hasn’t actually been announced at this point. The company hints, though, that it will be cheaper than the XPS 13 that already starts at $699 – in other words, Dell 14S might just be cheaper than the MacBook Neo.

	

The Dell 14S is available in the United States this fall. Pricing will be announced closer to availability in each market. What we can say is that the Dell 14S is designed to be complementary to XPS 13 and accessible for students and young adults globally. We’re committed to making sure regional pricing reflects that too.

Amusingly, Dell acknowledges that it already launched a laptop called the “14S” earlier this year, saying that the “old” one is designed for creators, while this “new” model “prioritizes everyday performance, long battery life, portability, colorful design and accessible pricing.” Perfectly not confusing.

title: Samsung’s latest Galaxy Book 6 starts at $799 with 8GB of RAM
snippet: Samsung is launching a new laptop in its Galaxy Book 6 series, and it’s much more affordable with a starting price of $799. more…
fullText:
Samsung is launching a new laptop in its Galaxy Book 6 series, and it’s much more affordable with a starting price of $799.

Announced this week, the latest Galaxy Book 6 release is a mid-tier version of Samsung’s laptop, cutting down on some key specs in order to hit a lower price point. Where the current lowest-priced option is a 14-inch (IPS) Galaxy Book 6 with 512GB of storage, 16GB of RAM, and an Intel Core Ultra 5 chip, the new model takes everything a step down with:

14-inch LCD display

Intel Core 3 or Core 5 processor

8GB or 16GB of RAM

256GB/512GB/1TB of storage

It’s a notable step down, but at considerable savings. Where that previously mentioned Book 6 starts at $1,249 in the US, this new release will start at $799 – $100 more than the MacBook Neo. 

The hardware measures in at 15.7mm thick, just shy of 3lbs, and has a 61.2Wh battery inside – Samsung claims 25 hours of battery life – with 45W USB-C charging. There are two USB-C ports, a USB-A port, an HDMI port, and a headphone/microphone jack. Samsung is also introducing a new “Violet Silver” color in addition to the usual grey.  It runs Windows 11 with Samsung’s usual suite of added apps that include a lot of integrations with Galaxy smartphones. 

	

Samsung’s new Galaxy Book 6 is available already in some markets, but not the US just yet. It’ll be available on Samsung.com and Amazon in the States starting October 5.

It’s officially the Ternus era at Apple.  

Tim Cook stepped down as CEO this week, handing the company to former hardware chief John Ternus, whose first memo promised a “huge launch next week” — timing that puts Apple’s next iPhone event on his desk before he’s even settled in. Cook isn’t going far, though: he’s staying on as Executive Chairman, focused on the kind of policy relationships that recently turned something as small as a map label into a very public balancing act. All of which raises an obvious question: what does the Ternus era look like, and how much rope will shareholders give him to figure it out?

 On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, hosts Kirsten Korosec and Sean O’Kane unpack what Ternus is walking into, why he may actually be better positioned to make progress on software than hardware in this new AI era, and more of the week’s news.

title: Apple Watch Series 12: Three new features coming next week
snippet: Apple Watch Series 12 is coming next week, launching at the September event alongside Apple Watch Ultra 4. Here are three new features rumored for Apple Watch Series 12. more…
fullText:
Apple Watch Series 12 is coming next week, launching at the September event alongside Apple Watch Ultra 4. Here are three new features rumored for Apple Watch Series 12.

#1: New S-class chip

Apple’s S-class chips don’t get meaningful updates very often. Even though Apple does change the number most years, actual CPU improvements are rare. And last year, the company skipped offering an S11 altogether and kept the S10 around.

But this year, rumors indicate an upgraded S-class chip is coming to Apple Watch Series 12. Likely named S12 or S11, it will be more powerful, faster, and also the first new Watch chip of the AI era.

Siri AI is a tentpole addition to watchOS 27, and it’s expected to run best on the new chip. But other everyday features should benefit from the new chip too.

#2: Always-on heart rate sensor and more health improvements

Apple Watch Series 12 has long been rumored to add new health features. For example, the FDA reportedly reviewed an upgrade to hypertension notifications that’s expected to debut next week.

One other specific rumor is that the heart rate sensor will get always-on support. This would match functionality offered by competing products like WHOOP.

Per Mark Gurman, the new Series 12 sensor can “continuously collect data throughout the day — not just when it senses you’re doing intense activity or at other random intervals.”

#3: Ceramic case option, likely in white and dark gray

Joining the usual new watch bands and case options, Apple is expected to debut a Ceramic case for the first time since 2019’s Series 5 model. 

Apple will reportedly offer Series 12 in two Ceramic colors: white and dark gray. Per Bloomberg: “Apple has tested both white and dark gray configurations for the Series 12 ceramic cases.”

It’s unclear how much of a premium Ceramic will add to the Series 12 price, but the last time it was offered, it started at $1,299—far more than Apple Watch Ultra costs today.

title: I Used the iPhone 17 Pro Max Without a Case for a Year. Here’s How It Looks Now
snippet: Apple promised improved durability for the iPhone 17 Pro, and its Ceramic Shield 2 protection might be the biggest durability upgrade in years.
fullText:
When Apple announced the new iPhones last year, it claimed to deliver “industry-leading durability.” However, within a few weeks of launch, the internet had a collective meltdown about the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max demo units looking scratched up in stores and a few units facing discoloration.

Reacting to the internet theories, Apple told CNET that the scratching was due to worn-out MagSafe risers, which transferred material to some iPhone models’ backs. (You could remove it by simply cleaning the back.) On the other hand, CNET’s Andrew Lanxon chemically treated his Cosmic Orange iPhone 17 Pro to test the discoloration claims.

	

			

He concluded that it “wasn’t going to be an issue for the vast majority of owners, and I don’t believe this can be considered any kind of fault on Apple’s side.” So I put my iPhone 17 Pro Max through 11 months of caseless use to find out how daily life affects its cosmetics. I didn’t put a case, skin or screen guard on it — just a ring stand on its back.

After almost a year of daily use with multiple accidental drops and pocketing with another phone, my cosmic orange iPhone is as cosmically orange as it was on day one (for the most part). There’s the expected color chipping and dents from drops, but the real surprise came when I put it against my iPhone 16 Pro (with similar usage). It helped put things in better context.

Here’s how my iPhone 17 Pro Max looks after a year of no-case use.

The Ceramic Shield 2 protection is real

The iPhone 16 Pro Max, on the left, is noticeably more scratched than the iPhone 17 Pro Max after a year of use without a case.Prakhar Khanna/CNET

The iPhone 17 models (and the iPhone Air) have an upgraded Ceramic Shield 2 protection for “3x better scratch resistance,” according to Apple. The 3x remark isn’t something you can instantly quantify. I could only see the difference when I put my iPhone 17 Pro Max next to my iPhone 16 Pro.

I used both devices for a period of 10 to 11 months without a screen guard. So they’ve gone through similar use: being kept in the same pocket as another phone, placed screen-down on a table and accidentally dropped.

My iPhone 16 Pro’s screen looks several times worse in comparison. It’s covered with scratches, both minor and deep. The soft scratches are gathered all over its cover glass. In contrast, the iPhone 17 Pro Max has a few minor ones here and there but nothing prominent. It looks pristine next to its predecessor. I can’t feel the scratches with my thumb on either screen, but the current-gen screen is smoother to scroll, while the iPhone 16 Pro feels comparatively rougher.

Ideally, glasses with better scratch resistance are prone to shattering easily, but my iPhone 17 Pro Max has fared far better than expected. I don’t have the exact number of times that I’ve dropped my phone; it’s slipped out of my pocket onto a bus floor, a marble floor, as well as onto concrete on the streets. I’ve dropped it from waist-height and my clumsiness has led to dents on its sides, but no screen damage. Each time I dreaded I had broken the display, my iPhone came out unscathed.

That doesn’t mean cracking is impossible — CNET’s Bridget Carey broke her iPhone 17 Pro Max’s screen soon after buying one after simply dropping it on the street. But from my time with it, I’m quite impressed.

Discoloration and color chipping

There are a few nicks on the phone, such as this small chip on the camera.Prakhar Khanna/CNET

Turning to the backside, the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max have Ceramic Shield protection instead of glass. The layer consists of nano ceramic crystals embedded in a glass matrix, which is, according to Apple, four times more resistant to cracks than the iPhone 16 Pro’s back glass.

While no two drops are the same, I’ve broke my 16 Pro when it fell on concrete flooring. The iPhone 17 Pro Max has managed such drops just fine. It has dent marks on the top and bottom right corners, but nothing worrisome. It’s survived more than I expected it would. To be clear, I don’t go around smashing my phones on different types of floor; it’s just hard to keep them in my hands (or pocket) when I’m on the road comparing two models.

While there’s some discoloration, none of the wear affects the phone’s functionality.Prakhar Khanna/CNET

Due to the nature of my work, I often carry multiple phones with me — usually with two in the same pocket. Possibly from rubbing against another phone, I notice there’s some color chipping on the edges of my iPhone 17 Pro Max’s camera island.

As for discoloration, over time, the cosmic orange polish has lightened in certain places. It’s most noticeable on the back side’s curved corners. There’s a permanent silver mark on the bottom-right side of my iPhone and a fading orange polish on the other side.

The corners show the most discoloration from my time using the phone without a case.Prakhar Khanna/CNET

It’s the only cosmetic change that I reckon has occurred from daily use and not one of those accidental drops. The magnetic ring stand I often attach to the back hasn’t caused any discoloration either. While it doesn’t cause any durability or usability issue, this is one thing to keep in mind if you’re planning to use a cosmic orange iPhone 17 Pro without a case.

Overall, I’m impressed with how my current-gen iPhone has aged in 11 months. The color chipping and dents were expected from my clumsy caseless drops. I also expected the screen to gather soft scratches all over its cover glass, but it surprised me in the best possible way. While some may want a case to truly protect the phone’s body, I’m glad that it simply looks a little worn from typical wear and tear.

While you may want a case to better protect the iPhone 17 Pro Max’s body, using it without one has largely left the display unaffected.Prakhar Khanna/CNET

But it’s the Ceramic Shield 2 protection on the display that provides the most noticeable durability upgrade. It’s fantastic how clear my screen still looks after nearly a year. If Apple continues to include it on the upcoming iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max models, they’d be the first iPhones I can confidently recommend using without any added screen protection.

title: Will the iPhone 18 Pro’s biggest upgrade really deliver?
snippet: In general, we’re not expecting the iPhone 18 Pro to be a significant upgrade over its predecessor. Indeed, if you currently have an older iPhone there are arguments for buying the iPhone 17 Pro ahead of next week’s launch. Of the few upgrades we are expecting, the biggest one on paper is going to be a variable aperture lens for the primary camera. But will this make a significant difference in reality … ? more…
fullText:
In general, we’re not expecting the iPhone 18 Pro to be a significant upgrade over its predecessor. Indeed, if you currently have an older iPhone there are arguments for buying the iPhone 17 Pro ahead of next week’s launch.

Of the few upgrades we are expecting, the biggest one on paper is going to be a variable aperture lens for the primary camera. But will this make a significant difference in reality … ?

Variable aperture offers control over depth of field

One of the biggest differences in the results you can achieve with a DSLR or mirrorless camera over an iPhone photo is control over the depth of field (DOF).

With a conventional camera, a wide aperture will create a shallow DOF that is most commonly used to separate the subject of the photo from the background. Portrait shots are a classic example (and this is why Apple’s simulated shallow depth of field feature is known as Portrait mode).

Conversely, when shooting something like a landscape or cityscape, you would typically use a narrow aperture to ensure everything is in focus from foreground to background. 

A variable aperture is therefore a standard feature of any conventional camera lens. iPhones, in contrast, have fixed aperture lenses. (There are some ways to achieve shallow DOF with an iPhone, and I’ll cover these in a separate piece after the launch of the new phone, but these are exceptions rather than the rule.)

A variable aperture iPhone lens

We’re expecting this is to be the year that the iPhone gets a variable aperture lens for the first time. It’s as yet unclear whether this feature will apply to both iPhone 18 Pro models or only to the Pro Max. Either way, it’s expected to be limited to the main camera, not the wide-angle or telephoto.

On paper, this is big news. In principle, a variable aperture lens allows us to control the depth of field. In practice, we shouldn’t get overly excited about being able to achieve the effect shown in the main photo above – and that’s because of what won’t be changing.

The bad news

The main limiting factor of iPhones is not the lens aperture – which is already rather wide – but rather the size of the sensor. Again, all else being equal, the larger the sensor, the shallower DOF you’ll be able to achieve. Compared to DSLRs and mirrorless cameras, iPhones have absolutely tiny sensors, and that isn’t going to change this year.

Given the same size sensor and a very slightly wider aperture, physics would suggest that we shouldn’t expect very much. 

The potential good news

There may be some reason for hope despite this. Including a mechanically variable aperture into one of the iPhone cameras is not a trivial task. It’s both complex and relatively expensive precisely because the lenses are so small. 

The question we have to ask, then, is why Apple would go to this trouble and expense for what we would expect to be a very marginal benefit? If it only delivers the kind of difference we would expect from the calculations alone, then it really doesn’t seem worthwhile.

That leads me to suspect that – if Apple really is going to make a marketing point of this new feature – then the company must have something up its sleeve. 

One possibility that strikes me is that the optical upgrade may be used almost as cover for a significant improvement to Portrait mode. While the simulated effect has grown better and better every year, there is still room for improvement, and perhaps the AI power of the upgraded chip has enabled Apple to produce something significantly more natural-looking?

If so, I doubt many people will care that it would be something of a cheat – the variable aperture providing a marginal benefit while the software delivers a far more meaningful one. What’s going to count for most people is the end result. This, then, is my best guess so far.

Do you have a better theory? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

title: Pixel 11 series getting early September update, not Android 17 QPR1
snippet: We’re expecting the stable release of Android 17 QPR1 in September. Before that, Google is rolling out an out-of-cycle update to the Pixel 11 series with a September 2026 security patch. more…
fullText:
We’re expecting the stable release of Android 17 QPR1 in September. Before that, Google is rolling out an out-of-cycle update to the Pixel 11 series with a September 2026 security patch.

On Tuesday afternoon, Pixel 11 series users received an OTA update to CD1A.260905.001.A1 (from CD1A.260714.001.A9). 

The Android security update level is “September 1, 2026.” (Note: Not September 5.) The install screen has the usual generic security message: “This update fixes critical bugs and improves the performance and stability of your device.”

So far, we have reports of an under 100 MB OTA hitting the Pixel 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL, and 11 Pro Fold. Google has yet to post factory or OTA images as of Tuesday afternoon.

	

This is not Android 17 QPR1. Several of the visual changes coming in that release are not yet present, so this is still the initial release of Android 17.

Rather, Google is likely rolling out this update as a hot patch for Pixel 11 issues discovered since last month’s launch. The fact Google did not wait for Android 17 QPR1 should be telling.

Following Magic Pointer and Desktop Camera, Google has now released a “Look up” app for Googlebooks. 

Look up lets you “highlight a concept you want to explore, a new word, a trip destination, and more.” This opens a floating window, with screenshots showing a dictionary, flight tracker, “Overview,” and translator. The “Ask a follow-up question” field at the bottom provides a conversational Gemini experience. The Play Store icon is a pair of glasses badged by the Gemini spark.

Google explains that “Look up will use publicly available information from the relevant Google service (e.g. Search, Maps, Flights) to provide the best response in a helpful format.”

The desktop interface and package name — com.google.android.desktop.contextualtools — make it clear that this is for Googlebooks, though the app can be installed on phones as of today. 

	

When you highlight text, “Look up” will appear as a menu option. This brings up the floating panel with results. Google will presumably close this unintended availability on phones in short order.

Look up is roughly analogous to a similarly named macOS feature (“Look Up”) when you right-click.
